# DEDICATION.

...born <note>This completes the word "nati" from the previous page.</note>, rely on virtue alone; nevertheless, those are to be judged far more fortunate and blessed than either who join virtue <term>virtus: in this context, both moral excellence and the traditional Roman concept of manliness and merit</term> to the splendor of their birth, and who strive to make that high rank <note>original: "fastigium"</note>—which they achieved through the good fortune of their birth—far more illustrious through noble deeds. And since this good fortune has fallen to **YOU, MOST ILLUSTRIOUS LORD**, you deservedly turn the eyes and minds of many toward **YOU** for this reason. 

How far removed from our age the origin of **YOUR** most splendid family is, how unsullied and undiminished the honor of nobility <note>original: "nobilitatis decus"</note> has been preserved within it, and furthermore, how great is the dignity in Germany of the knights who are subject at least to the Holy Roman Empire <note>original: "imperio Romano-Germanico"</note> itself—these things can be unknown to no one, unless they are entirely ignorant of the affairs of our fatherland. Since all these things are usually held in the highest regard by others, and are certainly not to be despised...

...are <note>The previous page ended with the catchword "be," (from the Latin *despicienda sint*), completing the thought that while noble birth is not to be despised, it must be matched by character.</note>, but are to be counted among the most extraordinary and beautiful ornaments that fall to anyone by the gift of God; yet by **YOU**, who look toward higher and more solid things, they are not held in such high esteem that you do not prefer, in many ways, those honors which are acquired through virtue <term>virtus: moral excellence and the merit earned through action</term> and erudition <term>eruditio: deep, systematic learning or scholarship</term>. You have many witnesses to this fact—namely, everyone who knows **YOU**—yet perhaps none of longer standing, or to whom all things are more thoroughly known, than myself. 

Twenty years have already passed since you first became known to me in this very academy <term>academia: a university or place of higher study; here likely the University of Jena</term>, in which you so devoted yourself to those exercises by which noble youth <note>original: "generosa pubes"</note> are usually occupied, that you nevertheless gave the first place to the study of letters, and gave a significant sign <term>praesignificatio: a foretelling or early indication of future character</term>—not a vain one—to the more perceptive of what kind of person you would become. ...who held you in high regard <note>original: "ferebant in oculis," literally "carried you in their eyes," an idiom for great affection or high esteem</note>, among whom it is permitted to celebrate, even after his death, **GEORG SCHUBART** <note>Georg Schubart (1650–1701) was a celebrated professor of history, eloquence, and law at the University of Jena.</note>, a man not merely lightly tinted by the more elegant letters <term>litterae elegantiores: the humanities, encompassing classical literature, rhetoric, and poetry</term>, but deeply imbued with them. It was for this reason you were accustomed to follow him with great veneration, and you still follow him now, though he is deceased. Nor do I consider it any less an honor to myself that I know my own efforts, such as they are, were not entirely displeasing to that great man. 

To me, indeed, by the will of the Divine Power <note>original: "Numine"</note>, it was soon necessary to depart elsewhere, and it did not enter my mind that we were to be joined together again. ...from the conversations which you frequently held with me. However, it pleased **YOU** to choose me as your guide in historical studies. In this field, I have labored with all my strength to show the way both to **YOU** and to certain other young men—distinguished by the splendor of their noble birth and the antiquity of their ancestors, and born for the hope of the fatherland. 

From this labor I reaped this fruit among others: that from that time our souls have been joined together, as if bound by the tightest possible bond. This, at least, seemed too bitter and sad to me: that I was soon to be deprived of **YOUR** presence, as the fates drew **YOU** toward other, indeed greater, matters.

# DEDICATION.

...your roles were to be. What followed from this point onward—with Divine Providence <term>Numen: refers to the divine will or the guiding power of God</term> most wisely directing all things so that the church, and perhaps even this academy <note>The University of Halle, a major center of the German Enlightenment and Pietism where the author was likely based.</note> itself, might derive more abundant fruit from it—since these things are manifest and open to the eyes of all, I will not recount them at greater length at this time. For more than once, **MOST NOBLE SIR**, I have expressed my thoughts on this matter, when it was granted to us to delight ourselves with the most pleasant recollection of past events. # PREFACE

<meta>catchword: Cum-</meta>

[...those holding this opinion] <note>The word "tientes" is the suffix of "sentientes," continuing from the previous page's discussion of those who hold specific philosophical views.</note> maintain, provided it is correctly understood, that whatever right <term>ius</term> <note>The Latin "ius" encompasses both "law" and a "right" or "authority" over others.</note> a human being has over any things whatsoever—whether over brute animals <term>bruta animantia</term> or other humans—all of it must be acknowledged as received from God. Furthermore, what we have asserted or conceded must be understood in this way: that by the name of "right" <term>ius</term>, there is generally designated a certain faculty <term>facultas</term> <note>In this context, a "faculty" is a legal power or capacity to act.</note> of acting lawfully and with **moral effect** <term>effectu morali</term> <note>original: "effectu morali"; this refers to an action that is not just physically possible, but creates legal or ethical obligations.</note>. While this faculty, if you look to its first origin, is certainly from God, it is nevertheless brought into action or exercise in various ways by humans themselves. Humans are deservedly considered the causes of this act or exercise, as well as of those things which follow from this act or exercise **.

---

** Indeed, if that phrase—"whatever man has, he has from God"—were to be understood as meaning that man himself could be the cause of no effect, whether by moral or physical reasoning <term>physica ratione</term>; or, what amounts to the same thing, that all things which belong to man by both physical and moral reasoning were held **immediately from God** <term>immediate a Deo</term> <note>original: "immediate a Deo"; a theological distinction meaning God acts directly without human mediation.</note>, it would follow that parents could not be called the causes of their children, and that children [come] immediately from God...

->TO THE READER.<-

Since for the exercise of this faculty <term>facultas</term> <note>In legal and philosophical terms, a "faculty" is the power or capacity to perform a specific action.</note>, or so that it may be brought into action by us, other people must sometimes also concur, it is manifest and most correctly stated that this faculty is brought into action in two ways: either without the consent of others, where it is not necessary, or with consent, where it obviously ought to be present. <sig>b 4</sig> <meta>minion-</meta>

---

[...to be] produced. <note>The word "progigni" at the top of the page completes a sentence from the previous leaf, likely referring to how rights are "born" or "produced."</note> Indeed, if this were not so, all **secondary causes** <term>caussae secundae</term> <note>Secondary causes are the natural means or human agents God uses to achieve a result, rather than acting through a direct miracle.</note> would be excluded—an opinion that the most acute philosophers have long shown brings great inconveniences with it. Thus, when **John the Baptist** says: *No one can receive anything unless it has been given to him from heaven* (John 3:27), the meaning is this: no one can take anything for himself by his own authority, but he must wait for a **calling** <term>vocatio</term> from God. However, it does not follow from this that the power <term>potestas</term> <note>Here, "potestas" refers to the formal power or office held by a person.</note> (for example) of **teaching and baptizing**, which is the subject of that passage, is always granted **immediately** by God, since this also happens **mediately**. And he who is called mediately <note>To be called "mediately" means to be appointed through human institutions (like the church or government) which act as God's instruments.</note> by God takes nothing for himself; rather, he has received his power from God no less than the one who was called by Him immediately.

### PREFACE

[do-]minion, and finally, in relation to other men, it is usually called **authority** <term>imperium</term> <note>original: "imperium"; while often translated as "command" or "sovereignty," here it refers to the lawful power one person holds over another.</note>. These things are plain and, if correctly perceived, admit no doubt.

Regarding dominion, the matter is clear for the reason we have stated: that it draws its origin from God. Scripture testifies to this expressly. For when God had created the first parents of the human race, He also granted them the faculty of using created things for their own preservation.
<margin>Genesis 1:28, 29</margin>
This grant was repeated for **Noah** and his descendants during the restoration of the human race. <margin>Genesis 9:2</margin> If anyone wishes to call this power of using created things for one’s own preservation "dominion," I shall allow it, provided that it is understood as a **common and universal dominion** <note>This refers to the theological concept that the earth was originally given to all of humanity collectively, rather than as private property for individuals.</note>. For if a possession of the kind from which others are actually excluded is understood, the word "dominion" will not be applied suitably enough.

Whatever the case may be, in order for this faculty to be put into practice, or for **private ownership** <term>dominia particularia</term> <note>Literally "particular dominions," referring to the transition from collective use to individual property rights.</note> to be introduced, it was entirely necessary for some external act to be added. And while there are some who believe this was done through division and agreements, it seems to us both simpler and more suited to the nature of the human race (as its state was then) that it was done through **occupation** <term>occupatio</term> <note>In historical law, "occupation" is the act of taking possession of something that belongs to no one with the intent of becoming its owner.</note>. And since this is by far the most manifest point, it follows from there of its own accord—

But you might say, "He did not, however, have authority over himself." This is entirely a play on the word *authority*. He did possess the faculty of directing his own external acts. While he renounced this faculty, he transferred it to another by his own **consent** <term>consensus</term>. And this very faculty of directing external actions is called at one time *liberty*, and at another *authority*. It is *liberty* if the man himself enjoys that faculty of directing his actions; it is *authority* if he has consented that it reside with another. 

However, because of the depravity of mankind, this power cannot remain with another constantly and effectively unless that faculty of directing the actions of others is also joined with the power of coercing those who are reluctant. Therefore, it is absolutely necessary for this coercive power to be added to authority properly so called, whereas in liberty, or the faculty of directing one's own actions, it has no place...

For since punishment is something inflicted against one's will, and yet what someone does to himself cannot happen against his will, it can only be explained with difficulty how anyone could have the power of punishing himself and be able to transfer it to another. 

When he had developed these points more extensively, he finally responds: "Here, therefore, it must be known that, just as in the natural world, from the mixing and tempering of several simple elements, a compound can emerge which possesses such qualities as are found in none of the simple elements entering the mixture; so also **moral bodies** <term>corpora moralia</term> <note>In 17th-century philosophy, a "moral body" refers to a group of people acting as a single legal entity, like a state or a corporation, which has rights and powers that the individual members do not have on their own.</note> consisting of several men..."

...deration <note>This continues the sentence from the previous page: "From the consideration of human nature also—"</note> it is easily understood that it is very fitting <note>original: "conueniens admodum"</note> for that which is commanded by God to be commanded, and for that which is forbidden to be forbidden. And although it is true that truth and falsehood by their very nature conflict with each other—so that what is true cannot be false, just as conversely what is false cannot be true—and by the same reasoning, what is good cannot be evil, and vice versa; there nevertheless remains the question: from where does the **obligation** <term>Obligation (*obligatio*): The moral bond or "tie" that makes an action a duty that must be performed.</term> arise to embrace the good or to flee from evil? 

And although the fact that **contradictories** <term>Contradictories (*contradictoria*): Two statements or qualities that are mutually exclusive; they cannot both be true or present in the same thing at the same time.</term> cannot exist together must be sought from the very nature and character of things, one should not judge in the same way regarding morality, or the idea that something is good or evil with a moral effect. 

There are also other questions: can something that is good be simultaneously evil? They must flee to him with true faith, inasmuch as he was sent by God for this purpose: that by his own blood he might expiate the crimes of men and earn for them divine grace. Assisted by this grace, they might finally be able to free themselves from those bonds of **perverse desires** <note>original: "prauarum cupiditatum"</note> by which they were held captive.

When, by this reasoning, they have changed their mind and will, they must seriously labor to ensure they do not contract new vices from the contagion of the world, or fall back into their former crimes. Instead, through prayers and other spiritual exercises, they should resist their cravings—repeatedly taking up this new **yoke** <note>A reference to the "easy yoke" of Christ mentioned in the Gospel of Matthew, representing the disciplined Christian life.</note> to tame and subdue their desires. In this way, they may lead the way for all as examples of self-control, modesty, patience, endurance, justice, equity, and the other virtues that are especially necessary for **civil life**. 

This is the sum of both the religion and the discipline of Christians. Is there anything to be found in it that is contrary to the **civil state** or to the safety of the **republic**? Everything tends toward this: that with their desires bridled, men may live purely, temperately, piously, and justly.

§. VII. And so indeed the Christian religion instructs subjects and citizens to duly fulfill the duties of their station. The Romans were indeed harassed by their enemies with impunity, and "square things were mixed with round" <term>original: "quadrata miscebantur rotundis" — a quote from the poet Horace meaning that everything was turned upside down or thrown into total chaos</term>, with both divine and human laws trampled underfoot, while the Emperor in the meantime vigorously indulged his own whims <term>original: "genio suo... indulgente" — literally "indulging his own genius," an idiom for prioritizing one's own physical pleasures and appetites above all else</term>.

Few men, perhaps, are found in history with such idleness and softness that they can be compared to Gallienus and his ilk. ### §. I.

There is no truth so manifest that the wickedness of mortals cannot endure to cast a mist over it. And so it is not surprising that the Christian religion has been slandered—both in the past as being opposed to the civil state, and even today by certain wicked and ill-advised masters of that "foolish wisdom" <note>An ironic reference to the idea that political cunning is a form of worldly wisdom that is actually foolish in a moral or divine sense.</note> which **MACHIAVELLI** <note>Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527), the Italian political philosopher often accused by theologians of separating statecraft from Christian ethics.</note> professed. Whether these things are said correctly, and whether MACHIAVELLI <note>Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527), the Italian diplomat and philosopher whose work *The Prince* and *Discourses on Livy* were often viewed as "profane" or amoral by later religious scholars.</note> truly thought so, I do not wish to inquire more lengthily now. Nor does a man of mediocre learning deserve that we should be so concerned about his opinion, for it is well-established that he treated civil doctrine with a profane mind.

It is enough if it is granted—even to the highest degree—that things are as he says, that he has still erred shamefully. He erred when he supposed that the happiness of a republic consists in a prince being able to propagate the borders of the empire far and wide; he erred when he thought that a prince should be called "happy" who is able to satisfy his depraved desires at will; he erred when he judged that republic to be happy or long-lasting whose citizens are warlike; he erred when he believed that men are made brave and despisers of danger not so much through true virtue, which the Christian religion inculcates and reconciles, but rather through the desire for honor, glory, and most vain things; he erred while he [suggested] to himself and others—

Let those foolish men go now and chatter about their **MACHIAVELLI**, those who value the tasteless comments of a wicked man more than the decrees of both right reason and the Christian religion. Let them boast of their "excellent teacher"—if the gods allow it!—this "politician" <note>The term *politico* was often used pejoratively in the 16th and 17th centuries to describe someone who prioritized statecraft over morality or religion.</note> who builds what he asserts upon such slippery foundations.

And if these things are observed, all is clear and straightforward; there is no need for the kind of evasions that **SAMUEL PUFENDORF** <note>Samuel Pufendorf (1632–1694) was a preeminent German jurist and philosopher who attempted to reconcile natural law with Protestant theology. Yet all this accusation will vanish instantly, provided the cause is explained which drove the Gentiles to throw such a thing in the Christians' teeth. To be sure, among the formulas for taking an oath, that one was especially accepted among the Gentiles by which one swore by the genius of the prince. If the sense of this formula were not that the swearers believed a divinity resided within princes while they were still living, or that they were calling down the princes' anger upon themselves if they were deceitful—but rather that they placed the safety of the prince before their own, and thus considered it a greater matter of religious duty to call God’s wrath upon the prince's head than upon their own—then perhaps it could be tolerated in some way. But in truth, that the Gentiles intended something else by this formula is evident even from the oath prescribed for Christian soldiers, which **VEGETIUS** (n) records: *they swear...*

### THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION AND THE CIVIL STATE

<page-num>59</page-num>

...[we lack the strength of] nations of particular places and their own borders, rather than those of the whole world? CYPRIAN supports TERTULLIAN: (e)
> *Therefore, none of us, when apprehended, resists, nor do we avenge ourselves against your unjust violence, although our people are numerous and abundant. Our certainty of future vengeance makes us patient. The innocent yield to the guilty; the guiltless acquiesce to punishments and tortures.*

(g) Lest I conceal anything, however, a learned man, DAVID BLONDEL <note>A prominent 17th-century French Protestant scholar and clergyman.</note>, (h) brings forward certain examples to the contrary. *Dionysius of Alexandria,* he says, *when an attack was made on the pagans who were leading him away, peri-* <note>The text breaks off mid-word; "peri-" likely begins *periclitatus* (was endangered) or *perierat* (had perished).</note>

### §. I.

It has been demonstrated in such a way that no doubt can remain for anyone regarding this matter: that the nature of the Christian religion is such that it contributes greatly to the preservation of the civil state. Perhaps, however, someone might be led to the opinion that this quality is shared by the Christian religion and those followed by the Gentiles <note>The author uses "Gentiles" to refer to the ancient Pagans of Greece and Rome.</note> and the Muhammadans. Therefore, to dispel this error, it will be helpful to compare the tenets of both the Pagans and the Muhammadans with the Christian religion, and to investigate briefly whether the commonwealth derives greater utility from those than from this. This investigation, while useful and pleasant, cannot but be highly honorable to the Christian religion.

*And they worship [them], yet no one is so thoughtless that he does not understand that they were merely mortal. "How then," someone will ask, "were they believed to be Gods?" Clearly, it was because they were the greatest and most powerful kings; due to the merits of their virtues, or their services, or the arts they discovered, and because they were beloved by those whom they ruled, they were consecrated to memory. If anyone should doubt this, let him consider their deeds and actions, all of which both poets and ancient historians have recorded.* <note>This italicized passage reflects a common argument in <term>Euhemerism</term>, a theory that Greek and Roman gods were originally historical kings or heroes who were deified after death.</note> Indeed, kings could be consecrated both because of their power and the dignity of the office they held; furthermore, another motive might also influence some: namely, that once a belief in the divinity of princes had been fostered among the common people, they might rule all the more securely. Other facts clearly confirm what we have stated. No greater honor for virtue or reward for deeds performed illustriously for the fatherland could be established than the majesty of divinity; through this, others might also be inspired to bring honor to and defend their fatherland or the <term>republic</term>.

Furthermore, in the Roman Republic especially, the custom of increasing the number of gods in this manner was transformed into an instrument of dominion. While everything on every side breathed with the worship of the gods, public rites were performed so that the common people—whose minds are most captivated by external spectacles and amusements of this kind—might be more easily drawn in. And certainly, anyone who weighs the rites of sacrifice for themselves will easily understand that everything was designed to captivate the common people and ensnare them in the traps of <term>superstition</term> <note>In this context, the author uses "superstition" to describe the man-made religious ceremonies used by pagan rulers to control the masses.</note>, so that the <term>republic</term> <note>original: "respublica"; the state or common wealth.</note> might be all the more secure and safe. I do not determine here whether the Gentiles received the custom of adding feasts to their sacrifices—the method of appeasing the <term>Divine Will</term> <note>original: "Numen"; refers to the divine power or presence of a deity.</note>—from the Hebrews, or whether God instead tempered His law to the stubborn nature of the Israelite people by permitting them (perhaps following the example of other nations) to add feasts to their sacrifices, provided they were celebrated soberly and moderately. For it is well enough established that they did indeed add them. (q) For from wherever that custom first flowed, it could not have been anything but highly pleasing to those who thought it in the interest of the <term>republic</term> <note>original: "reipublicae"; the state or common wealth.</note> to lead the pleasure-seeking common people to attend public sacred rites. Indeed, how could it occur to those who solely pursued pleasures to desire any other religious rites, when those public ones so remarkably flattered their desires? For the same reason, so that men devoted to pleasures might lack nothing they could desire, games were also added to the public rites. Therefore, the teachers of the early church were unwilling for Christians to participate in games of this kind, both because they considered it in itself hardly worthy of the Christian name, and especially because they regarded games as a part of <term>idolatrous worship</term>. "Sacred Scripture condemned every kind of spectacle," says **CYPRIAN** <note>St. Cyprian of Carthage (c. 210–258 AD), an influential early Christian bishop and writer.</note>, (r) "when it did away with idolatry, the mother of all games."

I leave all these things to be discussed more accurately.

However, I add yet one thing. It seems that the <term>Gentile religion</term> <note>original: "religio gentilis"; refers to the polytheistic religions of the Greeks and Romans.</note> was extremely well-suited for civil uses for this very reason: that it strikes and captivates the senses themselves, and from there, it moves the minds of the <term>common people</term> <note>original: "plebeias mentes"; refers to the masses or lower classes who were not educated in philosophy.</note> all the more strongly. The true worship of God is performed with a pure mind, and those things which can or ought to be known about the supreme <term>Deity</term> <note>original: "Numine"; refers to divine power or the presence of a god.</note> are to be grasped not by the senses, but by the intellect. 

But the condition of most mortals—especially those who have not trained their minds for higher things through study and the liberal arts—is such that they take delight in vices and depraved desires, and they cling to the senses rather than the intellect. And since we easily believe that which is troublesome or unpleasant to be either superfluous and unnecessary, or false, while on the contrary, we believe that which is pleasing or which we willingly undertake to be true and necessary; it can certainly happen very easily that we prefer external worship—especially that which brings the most delight, such as that of the Gentiles—to internal worship, and that we prefer the knowledge and faith of the senses to the knowledge of the intellect. 

Indeed, since by nature we are clearly unfit and by far the slowest to provide internal worship—that is, to present a pure and upright mind to God—if we correctly measure the character of the human mind, it is inevitable that most people [fall] toward contempt for the Deity and [the neglect] of integrity... <note>The text cuts off mid-word "o-" (likely *obliuionem* or *odium*) to be continued on the next page.</note>

### § VI.

**NUMA POMPILIUS**, that craftsman in the devising of religions—as he is called by **ARNOBIUS** (z) <note>Arnobius of Sicca (d. 330 AD) was an Early Christian apologist who wrote "Against the Heathen" (Adversus Nationes) to defend Christianity and critique Roman paganism.</note>—received the sacred rites with which he wished his citizens to be imbued from the Albans and the Sabines. He also summoned many things from **Etruria**, the *"mother and progenitor of superstition,"* as the same **ARNOBIUS** says. The Etruscans (or **Tyrrhenians**, as they were also called) undoubtedly received a portion of their sacred rites from the peoples of the East, with whom they maintained trade. The reason is therefore clear why the religion of the Romans agrees in many respects with the theology and the manner of worshiping the Gods of other nations, especially those of the East. Moreover, who would doubt that **NUMA**, a most shrewd man, by comparing the sacred rites of various nations, selected those which he believed would be beneficial to his own state? My authority for this matter is **LIVY** (a) <note>Titus Livius, the famous Roman historian known for his monumental history of Rome, "Ab Urbe Condita."</note> on account of...

...access to the office of the priesthood was open. Romulus, says **DIONYSIUS OF HALICARNASSUS**, (c) *passed a law in which he ordered that priesthoods should not be for sale, but should be chosen from the individual wards <note>original: "curiis"; the curia was a traditional political division of the Roman people.</note>, from those who had already passed their fiftieth year, who excelled others in lineage, were distinguished by virtue, possessed sufficient wealth, and were of sound body.* The same may be gathered from **CICERO**. (d) All this was done quite shrewdly. For first, all religion would easily have been brought into contempt among the common people <note>original: "plebeios"; the lower social class of Rome, as opposed to the elite patricians.</note> unless those who handled the sacred rites excelled others in a certain dignity and the splendor of their office. For it is the nature of mortals to regard all things as trivial and cheap which they see handled by men of the lowest rank; conversely, they consider those things noble and sublime which occupy men of great dignity and authority. Furthermore, those were to be appointed to this office whose interest it was that those secrets of the sacred rites be covered up, lest they become cheapened, and so that a greater veneration for them might be won daily among the common people. Hence that saying of **VARRO** <note>Marcus Terentius Varro (116–27 BCE), a prolific Roman scholar and writer.</note> found in **AUGUSTINE**, (e) *the high priest does not wish the people to know all things. For it is expedient that cities be deceived in matters of religion.* <note>original: "non omnia pontifex nosse populos vult. Expedit enim, falli in religione ciuitates."</note> This was something that could hardly be expected from a commoner. Moreover, since in the administration of sacred rites the welfare of the republic <note>original: "salutis reipublicae"; refers to the safety and health of the state.</note> always had to be taken into account, a new reason is evident why access to these things was closed off to the commoners.

For this reason, it was a solemn custom for the Romans to always seek auspices whenever something was to be carried out. **DIONYSIUS OF HALICARNASSUS** (n) teaches that this custom was instituted by Romulus <note>The legendary founder and first king of Rome.</note> himself: *Romulus,* he says, *instituted this custom, so that no one...*

### §. VIII. 

Now, if we compare the religion of the heathens <note>original: "gentilium"; referring to non-Christian, polytheistic traditions</note> with the Christian religion, it immediately becomes manifest that the latter by no means employs so many evasions, so many arts, and so many "machines" arranged to deceive the simpler folk, as the former does, nor does it stand in need of them. Indeed, those buildings that are less firmly joined together require more props <note>original: "fulcris"</note>, and a religion deprived of a foundation has need of more inventions, rites, and ceremonies. Furthermore, it can easily be proved by many arguments that the religion of the heathens—however magnificent and prideful with its vast apparatus of ceremonies, and however shrewdly tempered to the civil state through a thousand fictions and frauds—not only yields greatly to the Christian religion in this regard, but is simply unable to achieve by any means what the Christian religion does. It is useful, then, to briefly point out what those things are which win this praise for the Muhammadan religion <note>a historical term used by European writers for Islam</note>, so that it may be easy for everyone to decide what they consider to be consistent with the truth in this matter.

§. X. First, that conviction about fate <term>fate: "fatum," referring here to the concept of absolute predestination or "Kismet"</term> seems deservedly to be mentioned here, which that most crafty impostor <note>the author uses this polemical term for Muhammad, reflecting the common 17th-century European view of him as a political manipulator of religion</note> instilled in his followers. *For the Turks believe that a fatal limit for each person is predetermined—as to the year, months, and day—which can neither be avoided nor delayed; and that no one dies before their fate arrives, even if they plunge into dangers and throw themselves into battles. They believe that fate does not come until the measure of one's time has been fulfilled. This decree is not changed, even if a thousand groans and sighs, whether in praise or complaint, come from the mouth; there is no flight from it, nor any place for resistance...*

To this end, they have long been accustomed to sow wars upon wars, and to treat one victory as merely the instrument for the next...

Those who do not weigh this matter carefully are easily led astray; because they cannot distinguish the core essence of the matter from the corruptions and fabrications of mortals, they reject what is actually very beneficial as if it were something harmful. Now that we have clearly demonstrated that the **Christian religion**—that pure faith, uncolored by human inventions—contributes greatly to the preservation of the **civil state** <term>original: *status ciuilis*; the organized political community and its governance</term>, who could doubt it any longer? 

However, if we look at religion as it has been dispersed and scattered among various **sects** <note>original: *sectas*; the author uses this to refer to various denominations or religious factions that have deviated from his view of "pure" Christianity</note>, and defiled in such a strange manner, perhaps a different judgment must be made. Yet, to the extent that it has been corrupted, it can no more be considered the Christian doctrine—that is, the teaching of Christ and his apostles—than an error or a lie can be considered the truth. 

Just as the **dogmas** <note>original: *dogmata*; established beliefs or doctrines held by a religious group</note> of those who have split into different religious groups are quite varied—with some coming closer to the truth while others drift further away—so must we judge those points of Christian doctrine that relate specifically to the state of the **commonwealth** <term>original: *reipublicae*; referring to the public welfare and the body politic</term>. In these matters, some have retained the truth or have not strayed far from it, while others, by contrast, have either lost it entirely or obscured it.

§. III. §. IV. Therefore, you might ask, is it such a great crime to kill a tyrant? On this point, **MARIANA** <note>Juan de Mariana (1536–1624) was a Spanish Jesuit historian and political philosopher. His defense of tyrannicide in *De rege et regis institutione* (1599) caused a scandal across Europe, especially after the assassination of King Henry IV of France.</note> will surely have many very distinguished and learned men here who support him, even from other schools of thought. To be sure, I know that not everyone agrees on what a citizen is permitted to do against a tyrant. My own opinion is this: if someone is truly a tyrant—one who, having cast aside all divine and human laws, prioritizes his own interests over the safety of the republic <note>original: *saluti reipublicae*</note>, and acts so outrageously that he exceeds the patience of the citizens, and does so so openly that no room for doubt remains for anyone—then he can be resisted to the point that his command is finally revoked and his power to do harm is taken away. At that point, he should be viewed as an enemy <note>The author uses the term *hostis*, which in legal tradition refers to a "public enemy" or a foreign combatant, implying the tyrant has lost the legal protections of a citizen or ruler.</note>; and as long as he does not cease his hostile plots, it would not be a sin to use against him whatever measures are necessary for the defense of the republic. In this way, the security of the good—and even of the wicked, provided they have not reached the ultimate stage of madness—is sufficiently protected, yet citizens are not left entirely exposed to the whims and cruelty of such unrestrained men. Anyone can now understand from what has been already said how far the opinion of the **Jesuits** departs from this view. § VIII. The second hypothesis of the Romanists, which is diametrically opposed to the peace of republics and the civil state, is that most notorious one: **that faith need not be kept with heretics.** <note>original: "de fide haereticis non feruanda." It must be added, moreover, that this error is so manifest that one must have renounced reason itself if they have allowed such a fog to cloud their mind.

§. XI. ### THE CHRISTIAN RELIGION AND THE CIVIL STATE

<meta>catchword: ne</meta>

...of the Church <note>original: *ecclesiasticae*</note>, [the Council] declares that no prejudice can be generated, or impediment provided, nor ought it to be, which would prevent a competent and ecclesiastical judge—notwithstanding the said safe conduct <note>A legal document granting a traveler protection from arrest or harm, historically used to entice "heretics" to attend trials.</note>—from inquiring into the errors of such persons, and otherwise proceeding against them as is due, and punishing them as far as justice advises, if they stubbornly refuse to revoke their errors, even if they came to the place of judgment relying on the safe conduct and would not have come otherwise; nor is the one promising it <note>The secular ruler, such as an Emperor, who issued the protection.</note> considered to have remained bound in any way by this, provided he has done what is in his power.

Indeed, the sum of this decree ultimately comes down to this: even if someone should come to the place of judgment fortified by a safe conduct from an emperor or some king, that person—notwithstanding that promise—can be killed if it so seems fit to the Pope. Therefore, the pledged faith <note>original: *fides data*; refers to the honor of keeping one's word or a legal promise.</note> must be broken: why? Because the Pope commands it. Why does the Pope command it? Because the one to whom the promise was made is a heretic. Therefore, faith given to heretics must not be kept.

Nevertheless, **NATALIS ALEXANDER** <note>Noël Alexandre (1639–1724), a French Dominican theologian and ecclesiastical historian known for his massive work on Church history.</note> cannot bring himself to believe that such a thing was sanctioned in this decree of the **COUNCIL OF CONSTANCE** <note>An ecumenical council (1414–1418) that ended the Western Schism but also condemned Jan Hus to death, despite the Emperor's promise of safety.</note>. ### POLITICAL DISSERTATION ON CONCORD

...so that [the judge] might conduct an investigation regarding heresy and other crimes against him, and judge the person, once convicted by lawful testimonies and documents, according to the canons <note>Church laws or decrees.</note>. What, indeed, is liable to reproach in this decree? Nothing at all; rather, it is entirely consistent with law <note>original: *iuri*</note> and reason. For indeed, powers of a distinct order, each of which is supreme in its own sphere and independent of the other—nay, one even more excellent than the other—cannot mutually hinder one another from the lawful exercise of their own duties.

Now, secular and ecclesiastical power are of different orders; each is supreme in its own sphere and independent of the other; indeed, the ecclesiastical power is more excellent and of a superior order. Therefore, the secular power can, by no pacts, agreements, or promises, bind or prohibit the spiritual power from delivering judgment in a case that belongs to the ecclesiastical court <note>original: *fori ecclesiastici*; the specific legal jurisdiction of the Church.</note>. Likewise, the ecclesiastical power cannot bind a layman <note>In this context, the author refers to a secular ruler or civil authority acting in a non-religious capacity.</note> from conducting an investigation and passing sentence on a civil matter.

I will not dwell now on discussing the opinions—which **ALEXANDER** has mixed in here as if they were consistent with his own internal principles, though they are erroneous and clearly repugnant to reason—such as the claim that ecclesiastical power does not depend on the secular, that the former is more excellent than the latter, and other such things of the same sort <note>original: *eiusdem farinae*, an idiom literally meaning "of the same flour."</note>. Nor will I now convict **ALEXANDER** of plagiarism, which would be easy to do, because he copied this entire response word-for-word from **BECANUS** <note>Martinus Becanus (1563–1624), a Jesuit theologian and controversialist known for his defense of papal authority against secular monarchs.</note>. (z) I shall at least bring forward that which pertains to the matter itself.

### CHRISTIAN RELIGION AND THE CIVIL STATE

Certainly, I admit that one power ought not to be hindered in its own acts by the other. I will grant this for the moment; but at the same time, I infer that the ecclesiastical order acts wrongly when it hinders the secular order in its own acts. To promise something, to provide security to an accused person, or to grant a safe conduct—these are secular acts. Whoever orders these acts to be void <note>original: *irritos*; meaning legally nullified or made ineffective.</note> surely hinders them.

You insist: it is one thing to promise something, another to promise it to a heretic, and so on. Therefore, these acts are void either because the matter concerns a heretic, or because the Pope <note>original: *pontifex*</note> so orders. For they are entirely void according to the decree of the council. If it is because the matter concerns a heretic, then I have what I want: namely, the claim that no faith is to be kept with a heretic <note>original: *nullam servandam esse fidem*; this refers to the controversial medieval principle that a promise made to a religious dissenter was not legally or morally binding.</note>. If, however, it is because the Pope orders it, then in civil acts the prince depends on the Pope—which is again absurd <note>original: *absonum*; literally "out of tune" or inconsistent with reason.</note>.

For although who may be a heretic might perhaps be defined by the sacred order <note>the Church authorities</note>, yet to punish this man, or to provide security for him, are civil acts. You object: "the prince can keep his word, provided he does not hinder the judgment of the ecclesiastical power."

First, I invert this: the ecclesiastical order can exercise its own rights, provided it does not compel the prince to break his given word. Second, it seems to me that **ALEXANDER** <note>Natalis Alexander (1639–1724), a Dominican theologian and church historian.</note> is either joking or acting foolishly while he calculates his arguments in this way. For the prince gives his word to the heretic for this reason: so that from every assault both civil...

### CHRISTIAN RELIGION AND THE CIVIL STATE ###

...and those laws which are believed to depart from the honor due to the universal apostolic see <note>original: "universaeque sedi apostolicae"</note> must be considered entirely according to the doctrine of the Roman church itself. Indeed, the doctrine regarding the power of the pontiff <note>The Pope.</note> over the temporal affairs of kings and princes is, as I believe, most clearly evident from what has been said so far. If anyone should doubt that this doctrine is harmful to the state, and least of all to be tolerated by kings and princes, I would openly declare that person to be devoid of all reason.

§. XVII. I could add to these yet other reasons by which I might prove that the doctrine professed by the Romanists <note>The term "Romanists" was often used by critics to describe those who prioritized the authority of Rome and the Pope over national interests.</note> is extremely ruinous to states. For who is unaware that the Romanists possess more than one method for plundering citizens of their wealth and transferring it to the sacred order? I should mention here the marketplace of indulgences <note>The practice of granting the remission of temporal punishment for sins, often in exchange for financial contributions.</note>, dispensations regarding prohibited degrees of marriage, pious causes, the solemnities of masses, and whatever fraudulent arts Rome has devised to amass riches—wealth which the state must certainly go without. ## §. I.

The thickest fog of errors that weighed upon the Christian world, which was dispelled with such happy success by the labor of that great man MARTIN LUTHER, escapes no one's notice; and we also, as often as we recall it, rightly rejoice and congratulate ourselves. This benefit of that most blessed man is supreme, by which he deservedly holds many peoples bound to him in gratitude, and which the Blessed Balthasar Bebel <note>original: "B. ->CHRISTIAN RELIGION AND THE CIVIL STATE<-

...of the Christian religion, so it is also primarily adapted for the preservation of civil government. The following points of doctrine, which the **Lutherans** profess, are especially recommended, or rather, are those most relevant to this matter: (c) namely, that they assert the **magistrate** <note>The civil authority or government</note> is a divine ordinance; indeed, that it is established immediately by God. They hold that the majesty or power of a king is not rooted in the people <note>This denies the "social contract" theory that power originates from the populace, favoring instead the "Divine Right of Kings"</note>, and that he is the highest vicar of God on these lands, nor is he liable or subject in temporal matters to either the Roman Pontiff <note>The Pope</note> or to any other person.

Furthermore, they believe that the external care of sacred things—the <term>external episcopal right</term> <note>original: "ius episcopale exterius"; the legal authority of a secular ruler to oversee church administration and organization without performing spiritual duties like the sacraments</note>—belongs to him. Thus, he also has the power to convoke councils, call ministers of the church, remove them, and arrange rites and ceremonies. They also teach that no one is exempt from the jurisdiction of the magistrate, whether they be clergy or laity, and that subjects can never be released from their **oath of loyalty**. Just as it is a sin to resist the magistrate, they argue that not even a tyrant, in the exercise of his power, can be killed with impunity. To these points is finally added that, against an attacking prince, some Lutherans do not even admit the <term>limitation of blameless defense</term> <note>original: "moderamen inculpatae tutelae"; a legal principle from Roman law allowing for proportional self-defense. Here, it implies the most radical stance of non-resistance even against an aggressive ruler</note>.

§. IV. As for myself, it is established beyond doubt that the doctrine we profess so favors **civil authority** <note>original: "civili imperio"</note> that no other in the whole world favors it more, nor could favor it more through the prescription of **right reason** <note>original: "recta ratio"; the philosophical principle that human reason, when used correctly, aligns with natural and divine law</note> or the authority of divine laws. Nonetheless, all the arguments typically used do not please me equally, nor do they seem to prove the point for which they were intended. For it is a vice of the learned that while they gather whatever they can to adorn or defend a cause, mixing weak arguments with strong ones, they seem to betray the cause rather than assert it. 

It is enough, as far as this part of the doctrine is concerned, that the **Lutherans** teach what **Holy Scripture** teaches: that the **magistrate** <note>The civil government or ruler</note> is a divine ordinance, and that he must be obeyed in matters that are lawful and honorable. Furthermore, they teach that the magistrate is not subject to any other human power, whatever it may be, and thus, supreme power over all men living in the **republic** <note>original: "respublica"; referring generally to the state or organized political community</note> must be entirely granted to him. This is what all our churches, their **symbolic books** <note>original: "libri symbolici"; the official confessional documents of the Lutheran Church, such as the Augsburg Confession</note>, and even the principal—indeed, all—the doctors of the church profess. Nor do they foster any other opinions that would oppose this view in any way. This is certainly sufficient for it to be asserted as the definitive opinion of a church.

...[usurpatio]ns <note>Completing the word "vsurpationes" from the previous page's catchword.</note>, there was a need for leaders upon whom the care of interpreting, of compelling obedience, and of keeping [people] in their duty would rest. He says that the apostles or disciples of Christ fulfilled the role of these leaders, though not with the same glory, for the apostles held the highest rank; the remaining multitude of the faithful—to whom no task of interpreting or guarding the laws was entrusted, as is customary in republics—were considered in the category of subjects. Therefore, [he argues] that the apostles received majesty from Christ, not as clerics or by reason of a priestly office, but as founders and governors of the churches—that is, by reason of a royal office; and for this reason, the successors of the apostles are not priests, but Christian princes. The essence of the Christian religion is to demonstrate true faith through good works, charity, patience, and the remaining virtues. To this end, I do not see why an external society would be required. Nor is it necessary that the name of "church" should impose such a requirement upon anyone here. For if many Christians live in one place, it certainly cannot happen otherwise but that they occasionally meet for praying, teaching, and performing other sacred acts; it was from such a congregation of the first Christians living in one place that the name of "church" began to be used. 

But from this, it does not follow that a certain [political] society is necessarily required: since it is manifest that many people can live in one place, meet together, and establish certain things among themselves by mutual consent, without there being any external society—especially one joined with <term>sovereign power</term> <note>original: "imperio." In this context, it refers to the legal right to command or exercise state-like authority.</note>—among them. Granted, therefore, that the word "church" was taken from the assemblies that are usually established in democratic cities, as **PUFENDORF** also observed (h), one must not immediately imagine <term>something political</term> <note>original: "πολιτικόν τι" (politikon ti). The author is cautioning against assuming that because the word for a religious gathering was borrowed from Greek civic life, the gathering itself must have the legal powers of a city-state.</note> in the congregations of Christians. For it happens quite often that words transferred to denote other things take on different meanings; and wiser men have long since warned that judgment must be made from the things themselves regarding the words, not from the words regarding the things. ...we have found that the word "church" there simply denotes a congregation or assembly, a meaning that also agrees perfectly with the nature of the matter itself. Regarding the Church Fathers and the writers of the early church, whose testimonies **HARTMANN** (i) cites, it should be noted: (1) that these writers frequently use metaphors, allegories, and figurative language. Thus, because they conceived in their minds a certain similarity between a city and the church, it is not surprising that they described the church using the name of a "city."

But it should by no means be inferred from this that they believed the church to be, properly speaking, a city or a <term>civil society</term> <note>original: "societatem civilem." In legal and political philosophy of this era, this refers to a sovereign political state.</note>. They used these expressions all the more freely because, generally being untrained in philosophy, they did not consider what problems might eventually arise from such phrasing.

Secondly (2), most of these writers were affected by a flaw innate to all humanity. Namely, representing spiritual things to oneself through the lens of civil affairs aligns well with human ambition and <term>self-love</term> <note>original: "philautia," from the Greek φιλαυτία. The author suggests that theologians enjoy describing the church as a "kingdom" or "city" because it gives their spiritual roles the same prestige as worldly government.</note>, for whom command, dominion, and power appear as truly magnificent things. And so, although these good men did not possess worldly <term>sovereign power</term> <note>original: "imperio."</note>, they easily allowed themselves to be persuaded to think of spiritual and ecclesiastical matters in terms of power, a city, and similar concepts. He [the opponent] believes that the legislative power cannot be denied to the apostles, since *by interpreting the laws of Christ, they behaved as if they were legislators.* But may that most distinguished man forgive me: it is one thing to pass laws, and quite another to interpret them. A person who interprets laws does not immediately act as a legislator. Thus, he believes that the legislative power of the apostles has been sufficiently asserted and established by his argument. Yet, these points have not been presented in such a way that they can draw me over to the author's opinion. Indeed, in turning over and over again the writings of the apostles, I see no example of a law actually passed by them. I see that they diligently emphasized divine laws, and to this category belongs everything they teach concerning the duties of all people. certain opinions are touted as being dangerous or harmful to the commonwealth <note>original: *respublica* — the state or organized political community.</note>. A second example can be added to this: the right of resisting rulers <note>original: *ius resistendi* — a key concept in early modern political theory discussing when it is legal for subjects to oppose a monarch.</note>. Indeed, if a ruler degenerates into a tyrant, turns all his counsels toward the destruction of the commonwealth, and shamelessly violates the fundamental laws to that end, no one—unless blinded by a lust for flattery—would deny that citizens may resist him, and even take up arms if they cannot provide for their safety in any other way.

God has commanded that we obey those who govern; nowhere has He commanded us to obey tyrants. Therefore, those who teach that obedience is not owed to such tyrants offer nothing that contradicts the divine will, nor do they detract in any way from the authority or sanctity of legitimate princes. Why did they prove their loyalty and devotion to him so earnestly for so long, even when the best opportunity to strip him of the kingdom...

Learned men have always judged the errors of their adversaries (the Anabaptists <term>Anabaptistae: a diverse group of radical reformers who practiced adult baptism; here specifically referring to the peaceful Mennonite branches</term>) more kindly, especially those errors concerning the use of the oath and the office of the magistrate <term>magistratus: a public official or civil governor</term>, all of which seem to have arisen almost entirely from a great lack of skill in making proper distinctions. Regarding the oath and the office of the magistrate, why do they err? Is it not because of a neglected rule: that an abuse does not take away the use? <note>original Latin: *abusu non tollente vsum*. This is a classical legal principle (abusus non tollit usum) meaning that just because something can be used wrongly does not mean it cannot be used rightly.</note> And is it not because they do not distinguish the abuse which often happens in oaths and magistracy from the legitimate office and use of both? Even if others abuse the freedom of swearing and the power of holding the magistracy, can there not therefore be a good use for both? To me, indeed, such errors seem rather to have sprung from a lack of skill in interpreting Scripture. But whatever the case may be, whether such opinions are dangerous or harmful to the state <term>reipublicae: the common wealth or civil society</term> is precisely what is now being most thoroughly debated.

Perhaps content with his own lot, a man might abstain from such duties; for it would be reckless to throw oneself into dangers. Furthermore, they believe that the administration of justice <term>iustitiae administrationem: the legal authority to judge and punish</term> belongs to the civil magistrate, but that under the law of the Gospel, all things are to be administered out of love. In this, he is certainly mistaken, since the Savior in those cited passages intends only this: that no dominion or power to compel others belongs to the apostles and their successors *as such*—that is, in their role as teachers. Therefore, no discussion is actually being held there regarding the office of the magistrate. Meanwhile, we easily grant him this point: that the office of the magistrate can be regarded by someone as divine and holy, even if they simultaneously believe that it is not profitable or expedient for them, or even lawful, to undertake it. # CHRISTIAN RELIGION AND THE CIVIL STATE

...the *word of the famous Augustine*: *To swear falsely is dangerous; not to swear is safe.* <note>original German: "Falsch schvveren, ist gefährlich, nicht schvveren, ist sicher." This quote from St. Augustine was a common touchstone for groups like the Anabaptists who sought to justify their refusal to take legal oaths by prioritizing spiritual safety over civic requirements.</note>

I have brought these points forward for this purpose: to make it clear that the Anabaptists—if not all of them, then certainly the more learned among them—proceed more cautiously and circumspectly in this matter than is commonly believed. Meanwhile, anyone can easily understand for themselves that this opinion can create no danger for civil government. For what truly is the need for an oath <term>oath<note>original Latin: "iureiurando". For the Anabaptists, the "oath" was a specific legal and religious ritual they rejected based on a literal reading of Matthew 5:33-37.</note></term> when citizens are endowed with such character that trust can safely be placed in them even without one? That such indeed are the morals of the Anabaptists could be proved even by the testimonies of their own adversaries, which they have experienced. 

And this is also the point urged by **VAN DOOREGEEST** <note>Angelus Arenston van Dooregeest (1651–1725) was a Dutch Mennonite teacher and author who wrote extensively in defense of Anabaptist principles against state pressure.</note>: *And so that we may not be an obstacle to a country or kingdom with this opinion, it is easy to grasp that the stability of a government consists not in the oath, but in the fulfillment of the required loyalty <term>loyalty<note>original German: "Treu". This refers to the "Fealty" or "Faith" a subject owes to a sovereign, which Van Dooregeest argues is a matter of behavior, not ritual speech.</note></term>, for the sake of which the weak means of the oath alone is used by some. But no one will be able to deny that such means are no longer necessary when the same end can be sufficiently achieved through other ways that are much safer. And what assurance of loyalty is better than the evidence of good loyalty itself?* 

Furthermore, he teaches at greater length, through the examples that follow, that the Anabaptists have not acted recklessly in such a way that a magistrate would need to demand an oath of them.

## Synopsis.
<note>original: Σύνοψις</note>

*There are two main pillars for all deliberations: honor and utility, § I. For the instinct of all living creatures, and even of man himself toward self-preservation, teaches that consideration must also be given to utility, § II. This is also observed in entire societies and states; those who were skilled in the art of preserving them were once called "the wise," § III. In more recent times, the <term>reason of state (Latin: ratio status)</term> <note>This refers to the justification for a state's actions to ensure its survival or benefit, often a controversial topic in political philosophy.</note> arose from this, though the term has various meanings, § IV. However, those who believe something can be useful without being honorable are greatly mistaken, § V. This can be proven by the example of treaties, the necessity of which is asserted, § VI. For these alliances must be entered into such that both honor and utility are taken into account within them, § VII. Hence, to clarify what the reason of state requires in treaties, one must first look toward honor, and then toward utility, § VIII. So that honor may remain consistent in treaties, one must first determine with whom it is lawful to enter into such alliances...*

->§. I.<-

<note>An ornamental woodcut initial 'C' is featured, decorated with floral motifs and a central circular design.</note> Since nothing can be undertaken rightly or prudently unless it is first diligently consulted upon—considering the method for making a decision and what must be investigated regarding any given matter—it is customary for these things to be defined thoroughly in the teaching of ethics. Panaetius <note>Panaetius of Rhodes (c. 185–109 BC) was a Stoic philosopher whose lost work *On Duties* served as the primary model for Cicero’s famous treatise.</note>, once a great master of the Stoic school, as Marcus Tullius Cicero reports, (a) claimed that there is a threefold deliberation in making a decision. For, he says, we deliberate whether a deed is honorable <note>original: *honestum*; referring to moral rectitude or what is "right" regardless of consequences.</note> or shameful; likewise, whether it contributes to the convenience and pleasure of life <note>original: *utile*; the "useful" or "expedient" aspect of a choice.</note> or not; and what must be done if honor seems to conflict with utility. Cicero himself, however, noticed that two things were omitted from this division, and cleverly—

# ON TREATIES.
<sig>Q 4</sig>

...very [eloquently], as he is accustomed to do, [Cicero] observes that not only can one deliberate whether a matter is honorable or shameful, but even when two honorable things are presented, which is more honorable? And likewise, when two useful things are presented, which is more useful? However these things may be, the person who reduces all deliberations and consultations to two main categories—honor and utility—will not go wrong. For once these are correctly defined, any comparison that needs to be made will proceed with ease.

->§. II.<-

That the consideration of utility <note>original: *vtilitatis*; referring to political expediency or what is advantageous for the state’s survival.</note> must also be maintained is proven by that instinct of nature by which all animals, and especially humans, are impelled and stirred toward their own preservation and the repelling of all things that are harmful to them. We have learned that the Stoics <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophy that taught that virtue is the highest good and that humans should live in harmony with the natural order of the universe.</note> taught there are certain "primary things of nature" <note>original: *prima naturae*; a Stoic term for the basic instincts, such as health and survival, that nature gives to every living thing before they develop the power of reason.</note> by which an animal, as soon as it is born, is reconciled and commended to itself for the sake of its own preservation, and for protecting its own state, and for loving those things that are preservative of its state. As **SENECA** <note>Lucius Annaeus Seneca (c. 4 BC–65 AD), a Roman Stoic philosopher and advisor to Emperor Nero.</note> excellently put it:

> *An animal is first reconciled to itself. No animal enters into life without the fear of death: for each thing is reconciled to its own safety at its birth; it seeks those things that help it and dreads those that will harm it.* (b)

§. III. Although these traits <note>Referring to the instincts for self-preservation mentioned on the previous page.</note> are found both in brute animals and in individual human beings, they are most conspicuous in cities and entire societies, where they present themselves to everyone's view. **CORNELIUS TACITUS** (c) <note>A famous Roman historian known for his analytical and often cynical accounts of power and politics.</note> records the "state of the city" <note>original: *statum urbis*</note> and declares that he will explain its reason and cause; at the same time, he suggests that there is an impulse inherent in cities by which they are driven toward their own preservation. Those who have a clear understanding of this reason and cause—that is, to express the matter in the words of **ARISTOTLE** (d), those who understand what the "end" or purpose of the city is and have learned to find the things that lead to that end—are called **wise**, a term suited to the character of the ancients. Again, I can cite **CORNELIUS TACITUS** as a witness who fully supports my view when he teaches that those things offered by chance must be turned into wisdom; he calls those skilled in this art *“wise and shrewd observers of the times.”* (e) <note>original: *sapientes & temporum callidos*; this refers to the political skill of adapting one's strategy to the specific circumstances of the era.</note> By this splendid and magnificent name, no others are designated than those who can rightly consult the interests of their fatherland and city and devise what is beneficial for it.

§. IV. ...tainly <note>The text continues from the previous page's discussion on the "wise and shrewd" who find "beneficial" paths for the city. But let such people be gone. Certain great men explain the whole matter more correctly; they invoke certain secret and more hidden—yet still honorable—methods for preserving and protecting the **commonwealth**. <note>original: *rempublicam*</note> The **utility of the city** <note>original: *utilitas civitatis*; the practical welfare or benefit of the state.</note> takes center stage <note>original: *utramque hic facit paginam*; literally "makes both pages," a Latin idiom meaning a subject is of primary importance or fills the entire discussion.</note> here; yet there is still a place for honor, though the goal is pursued by an unusual path, trodden by only a few. 

Because of this, it often happens that those who so carefully weigh the methods of their counsels seem to be committing many things wrongly or unfairly to those who have not learned to look into the true sources of events and actions. Prudent judges of affairs, however, feel otherwise. Indeed, those who reflect on the **Reason of State** <note>original: *status ratione*</note> in this way, and judge it as is fitting, are far from deserving the criticism of others.

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the nature of international agreements, transitioning from a critique of Utopian idealism (where treaties are seen as unnecessary) to the practical and moral complexities of the "Reason of State." ### CONCERNING TREATIES ###

<margin>In the *Sayings of the Spartans*</margin>
Plutarch <note>original: *TARCHVS* (OCR error for *Plutarchus*); a Greek historian and essayist.</note> mentions a man <note>The author refers to the Spartan general Lysander, notorious for his cunning and lack of scruples.</note> who was crafty and mixed much with deceit, placing justice in utility alone. He claimed that truth was no better than a lie, but defined the value and dignity of both by their practical use; he even boasted that children should be deceived with dice, but men with oaths <note>original: *sacramentis*; in this context, the sacred religious oaths taken to seal a treaty.</note>. Indeed, there are some who openly profess that it is foolish to enter into a partnership of other people's dangers, and thus believe that no one can be blamed if they refuse to stand by the laws of a treaty <note>original: *federa*; formal alliances or compacts between nations.</note> when they see it is no longer expedient for them.

§. VIII. Since this is the case, in my opinion, only those truly weigh what the **reason of state** <term>reason of state: (Latin: *status ratio* or *ratio status*) the political theory that the national interest and the security of the state should justify the means used to maintain them</term> requires who carefully examine first whether treaties are honorable, and then whether they are advantageous to us. From this, our dissertation naturally branches into two heads to be treated in order. Regarding that which is honorable and agreeable to divine laws, I see that many most learned men have given instructions. Yet I know that they have not infrequently allowed such things as ought to be and can be entirely corrected. However, it is at least our purpose to go through the main points and touch upon the principal matters that can be drawn into debate.

I consider it superfluous to inquire into the conduct of those who despise the Divine Being <note>original: *Numinis*; referring to God or the divine power that governs the universe.</note> and all that is honorable. To be sure, this capacity for consent can be hindered in many ways, and especially by the authority of a superior, if the person making the agreement has been placed under another’s command. But in the case of supreme rulers, whose role it is to enter into treaties, anyone easily understands that these restrictions have no place. 

I admit that rulers can sometimes bind themselves to such an atrocious crime that it is not a sin to deny them what one human being otherwise rightfully demands from another by law. Nor do I deny that it is a great crime if someone thinks of the Divine Being differently than is proper, or does not worship It as It ought to be worshiped according to the prescription of reason and revelation <note>The author refers to the two sources of knowledge in 17th-century thought: *ratio* (logic/natural law) and *reuelatio* (scripture/divine decree).</note> (to which reason leads). # ON THE STATE AND CONCERNING TREATIES.

I agree with **POLYBIUS** <note>Polybius (c. 200–118 BC) was a Greek historian of the Hellenistic period. He is often cited in political theory for his views on the stability of states and the moral character of nations.</note>, who judges: *to trust absolutely no one is to lose the ability to act or conduct affairs.* (d) Indeed, it is plainly foolish to attribute the loss of one's fortunes—a loss some suffer and which each ought to blame on their own fickleness—to the most sacred law of nature. Finally, for someone to demonstrate a noble character, there is always an opportunity at hand; therefore, the sanctity of pacts or treaties <note>original: *pactorum aut federum*</note> must not be called into doubt for that reason.

§ XIX. And treaties enjoy this sanctity even if they are not confirmed by an oath. **GUNTHER** <note>Gunther of Pairis (c. 1150–1220) was a Cistercian monk and poet known for his Latin epic "Ligurius," which celebrates the deeds of Frederick Barbarossa.</note> records a saying of the Emperor **FREDERICK BARBAROSSA**, in which he declared that *a king's word carries a right and a reverence greater than any oath.* (e) Certainly, it is so shameful to break one’s faith <note>original: *fidem fallere*</note> that no one can bring greater disgrace upon themselves than by staining their character with the crime of treachery <note>original: *perfidia*</note>. Indeed, the crimes of Princes are as much more conspicuous, and thus more shameful, as they themselves surpass others in dignity. Nevertheless, experience and practice have taught us that the faith of most princes is so slippery <note>The author uses the word *lubricam* (slippery or hazardous), suggesting that a ruler's promise is often difficult to hold onto without formal enforcement.</note> that, unless they have been bound by a tighter bond to keep it, no one can trust them. For this reason, we see that it has become the custom among most nations to confirm treaties with an oath. For the Romans rightly judged, as **CICERO** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC) was a Roman statesman and philosopher whose writings on "De Officiis" (On Duties) defined the Western understanding of oaths and promises.</note> testifies...

...as **CICERO** <note>Marcus Tullius Cicero (106–43 BC) was a Roman statesman and philosopher whose "De Officiis" (On Duties) was a foundational text for early modern political ethics.</note> testifies, *our ancestors intended that no bond for securing one's word should be tighter than an oath.* <note>original: *nullum vinculum ad adſtringendam fidem iureiurando arctius eſſe voluerunt*</note> He adds: *this is indicated by the laws in the Twelve Tables <note>The Twelve Tables (c. 450 BC) were the earliest code of Roman law, forming the foundation of their legal system.</note>, by the sacred laws, and by the treaties, through which faith is pledged even to an enemy.* (f) By these words, he teaches that an oath was utilized not only by men of private station, but also by princes and rulers of affairs, for the purpose of ending disputes and confirming promises. (g)

§ XX. While I assert these points, I do not however claim that a situation can never arise where it is permissible for either party to withdraw from a treaty. For if one party has violated the laws of the treaty, by the consensus of all, the other party shall also be released from them. Nothing more unjust could be imagined than if innocent men were held to stay by agreements which the wicked refuse to observe. Furthermore, mutual consent and mutual faith constitute a treaty <note>original: *fedus*</note>; therefore, if either party dissents and breaks that faith, the treaty itself vanishes like smoke <note>original: *in fumum abit*</note>. Hence, those who first violate its laws and conditions are deservedly accused of having broken the treaty. Some add that a party is also released from the law of a treaty when the status <note>original: *status*</note> of the state to which they were joined is changed. Conversely, the state itself, which undergoes the change, may be freed from the bond of the treaty. Because

# CONCERNING TREATIES

...I would not admit this lightly. For how far that idea shrinks from the truth has, I think, been understood by those who, in order to proceed more cautiously, believed that *real treaties* <note>original: *realia federa*; these are treaties tied to the state or "the thing" itself, rather than the individual leader.</note> ought to be distinguished from *personal* ones, as they are called. **HUGO GROTIUS** <note>Hugo Grotius (1583–1645) was a Dutch jurist whose work "On the Law of War and Peace" laid the foundations for modern international law.</note> diligently emphasizes this (h), and **JOHANN TESMAR** <note>Johann Tesmar (1643–1693) was a legal scholar known for his commentaries on Grotius, often used in academic disputations.</note>, who follows in his footsteps, has summarized in a few points those chapters which, as he believes, clearly indicate the difference between these types of treaties. (i) For if a treaty being entered into is commanded to be perpetual and eternal, and if it looks to the benefit of the whole state, or if mention is also made in it of successors and heirs, then he thinks it follows from an indubitable line of reasoning that the treaty is *real*. While these conditions are certainly such that they cannot easily be called into question by anyone, I nevertheless consider them to be plainly superfluous. A prince who enters into a treaty always represents the state while he negotiates it. If he does not represent the state, the agreement will be a private contract, or anything else rather than a treaty. Therefore, every treaty binds the entire commonwealth <note>original: *rempublicam*</note>, and whatever fate the city may undergo, it will be bound by the treaty; at the same time, the party who entered into the treaty with the state will also be obligated. However, as for the claim that treaties which rely upon a specific condition of the state expire when that condition is changed, that is by no means...

# POLITICAL EXERCISES ON REASON OF STATE <note>original: *EXERCIT. POL. DE RATIONE STAT.*; refers to "Ratio Status," the early modern concept of "Reason of State" where the interests of the state are the primary guide for a ruler's actions.</note>
