§. XXI. Regarding what is human and divine law <note>original: *ius fasque*; a common Latin pairing referring to secular or human law (*ius*) and sacred or moral law (*fas*).</note> in treaties, it shall suffice to have touched upon these matters. Now, let us pursue the heart of the case. For we must duly explain the path that supreme rulers ought to take so that they do not regret having struck treaties, as has happened to many. Indeed, the "stern and the prow" <note>original: *puppis vero atque prora*; a nautical metaphor meaning the beginning and the end, or the most essential parts of a matter—essentially the "sum and substance."</note> of prudence is achieved when we have thoroughly explored the spirit and the purpose with which someone approaches us to strike a treaty. Those who serve their own interests so exclusively that they care little for the fates of others cannot help but bring many great dangers upon us if they are joined to us by a treaty. But if we are further informed that it is greatly in their interest for us to be of no standing at all, then there is need for much greater circumspection. So great is the **lust for power** <note>original: *dominandi libido*; a phrase frequently used by Roman historians like Tacitus to describe the insatiable desire for political control.</note> in most men that it can be restrained or coerced by no law. Hence, nothing is more common than to oppress others who have been deceived by the sanctity of treaties.

§. XXV. Furthermore, treaties <note>original: *federa*</note> are for the most part entered into through ambassadors <note>original: *legatos*; these are the envoys or representatives sent by a sovereign.</note>. Since these envoys act according to the instructions of those who sent them, and everything that does not agree with those instructions is considered void, only he will properly observe the interests of his own state who has thoroughly understood what the ambassadors may actually promise and how far they may rightly negotiate. For those who place trust in promises that the ambassadors had no power to make are merely "grasping at clouds and emptiness" <note>original: *Nubes enim & inania prensant*; a classical idiom for pursuing illusions or hollow dreams.</note>. ### CONCERNING TREATIES ###

...but rather whether one who is soft and effeminate, or a great force of gold and silver, is being supplied.

§. XXX. Therefore, although supreme rulers rightly deliberate over the fortune of others, they should—with **QUINTUS CURTIUS** (i) as their judge—keep their own fortune in mind during their council. According to the saying of the Emperor Hadrian, they act imprudently who *lean against a falling wall*, (k) <note>original: *in caducum inclinant parietem*; a proverbial expression for relying on a state or person whose power is collapsing.</note> yet sometimes not only the principle of honor (as I have already advised) but also the condition of our own affairs most greatly urges us toward such an alliance. For what if someone desires to enter a treaty with you whose ruin, as **TACITUS** says, is bound to drag you down as well? (l) 

In this matter, however, I can by no means praise the advice of the otherwise most celebrated man **JUSTUS LIPSIUS** (m) <note>Justus Lipsius (1547–1606) was a highly influential Flemish humanist whose works on political "prudence" often blended morality with Machiavellian realism.</note>. *In that case*, he says, *either join yourself to them or help them, but what if you do so secretly? That is the old cunning: to openly put on the alliance of one side, while leaning more toward the other through secret and more faithful channels.* 

I judge this very behavior to be not far removed from treachery <term>perfidy: a deliberate breach of faith or "double-dealing" in international relations</term>. It is perhaps more rightful for one placed in such a critical state of affairs to join neither side, if it would be dangerous to openly defend the party of the weaker. In this way, he may nevertheless—provided the cause is just—succor the weaker party through some secret method and supply them with strength.

§. XXXI.

§. XXXI. Moreover, those do not always seem to me to suggest beneficial advice who desire that those to be joined in a treaty should be equal in strength and power. For although the mutual fear that exists between them seems to contribute much to the permanence of a treaty—since, as **THUCYDIDES** (n) <note>Thucydides (c. 460 – c. 400 BC) was an Athenian historian. His work is a cornerstone of "realist" political theory, which suggests that states act based on power and interest rather than morality.</note> says, *nothing makes an alliance faithful except mutual fear* <note>original: *societatem nihil aliud fidelem faciat, quam mutuus metus*</note>—nevertheless, it more often causes harm. And if rivalry <term>emulation: a spirit of competition or jealousy that often arises between two parties of equal status</term> should be added (and this is hardly ever absent), the treaty may be broken prematurely, and every benefit you hoped for from it will perish. 

Nor should anyone fear that, by this reasoning, no one will be found with whom a treaty can be properly entered into—as if neither those more powerful, nor the weak and less powerful, nor those equal in strength are to be admitted into an alliance. For the things I have asserted thus far must be understood with a certain balance <term>temperamentum: a moderating context or "middle way" that qualifies a general rule</term>. 

If someone is indeed more powerful, but their strength does not so far exceed our own that we have great cause for fear, such an ally will be most suitable for us to achieve the goal we have set for ourselves in the treaty. Likewise, when I command that the less powerful be kept away from treaties, I mean those who are equipped with so little strength that they depend solely on our help, while they themselves can be of no use to us. For it is possible for someone to be strong in resources, yet still yield to us in overall power.

# POLITICAL EXERCISES ON THE REASON OF STATE

...treaties which they entered into with us will have any measure of stability. Indeed, while we remain at peace, these agreements will be treaties in name only; but if our army should receive a heavy blow anywhere, a hostile hand will fall upon us without delay. This is first because they made terms with us not by their own will, but by the misfortune of fate and by necessity—and with a greater sense of shame than we feel. Secondly, it is because we have had many disputes arising from these very treaties. 

We have heard that the Emperor **MANUEL KOMNENOS** <note>Manuel I Komnenos (1118–1180) was a Byzantine Emperor known for his sophisticated, if sometimes pragmatic, diplomacy with the Crusader states and the West.</note> expressly denied that he felt bound to care for those agreements that had been promised under the pressure of necessity. "Doubtless," they say, "even in treaties, the middle path is not without danger." They argue that enemies should rather be removed entirely, or regarded as open enemies, than be joined to us by such a treaty that fails to actually turn them into friends. And their opinion would easily win me over as well, were it not so unjust. As it is, I judge it a wicked thing to immediately slaughter to the point of extermination those whom we cannot bind to us by a firm and lasting treaty simply because they have been cast into a worse fate. Therefore, the other path has always seemed safer to me: that a treaty be entered into on generous terms <note>original: "liberali conditione"</note>, so that no occasion is left for the allies to complain...

### §. XXXVII.

However, I by no means subscribe to the opinions of those who decree that all treaties entered into through fear are void. If that were the case, wars would be ended by solemn peace treaties in vain, since it is very rare for parties to lay down their arms as long as their forces remain equal on both sides. If, however, the forces are unequal, the fear of losing everything cannot fail to drive the weaker party to submit to the conditions of peace. 

Although the masters of <term>civil prudence</term> <note>Also known as "reason of state" or political science; the practical art of governing and diplomacy.</note> command that this fear be concealed—using that line from <term>Homer</term>: *I too have smooth spears and rounded shields* (e) <note>original: "et mihi sunt teretes hastae, clypeique rotundi." This is a reference to the *Iliad*, used here to suggest that a weaker party should pretend they still have the means to fight to gain better terms.</note>—it can never be so well hidden that it does not betray itself in some way. Meanwhile, it is in the interest of all men that peace treaties be kept sacred. 

I will not now disturb the decrees of the philosophers, nor will I touch upon their disputes regarding whether fear renders agreements void. Yet, I cannot fail to touch briefly on the point that settles the whole matter. Certainly, those who assert that agreements entered into without deliberate counsel, and in which true consent is lacking, are destitute of all binding power, say nothing...

...which they think is worthy of blame. For no agreement <note>original: *pactio*</note> can exist without consent. I also admit that a person cannot give consent if their intellect labors under a disease of such a kind that they cannot distinguish things with a true understanding; or if their will is restrained and deprived of the freedom in which it usually rejoices. Nor do I deny that the mind is often so disturbed by fear <note>original: *metu*</note> that we neither understand the reality of the matter, nor is it within our power to truly desire it. 

There are, however, certain degrees of fear. That fear which is joined with a sudden impulse and agitates the mind so violently that it "throws it from its seat" <note>An idiom meaning to lose one's reason or rational composure.</note>—this certainly stands in the way of our ability to consent, and thus renders every pact void. 

But after those more violent emotions have settled and our mind has returned to a calmer state, the fear that remains—arising from the sober consideration of an imminent evil—neither disturbs the power of the intellect nor deprives the will of all its freedom. 

If a man sees that he will be exposed to immense danger if he continues a war, and fear enters him because of this, he is by no means "forced" to lay down his arms in a literal sense. Instead, he freely decides within himself whether he wishes to risk his fortune and commit it to the <term>hazard of war</term> <note>original: *bellique aleae* — literally "the dice-roll of war," a common classical metaphor for the unpredictability of military conflict.</note>, or whether he prefers to ward off the imminent evil by a safer path—even through an agreement that is of little benefit to him. 

Therefore, such actions are usually classified as "mixed" actions <note>In Aristotelian ethics, a "mixed action" is one performed under pressure where the person chooses the lesser of two evils; it is considered voluntary because the person still makes a choice.</note> by the teachers of <term>moral philosophy</term>, so that...

<summary>This page argues that while extreme panic may invalidate a treaty, a calculated fear of military defeat does not destroy a leader's free will or the validity of a peace agreement. It distinguishes between irrational terror and the rational choice to accept a disadvantageous peace to avoid total destruction.</summary>

### Section XXXVIII. ###

We have not yet sufficiently provided caution for those about to enter into treaties. "The most sacred thing," in the opinion of <term>Jean Bodin</term> <note>Jean Bodin (c. 1530–1596) was a French jurist and political philosopher, best known for his theory of sovereignty.</note>, (g) "is the society and faith which king gives to king, man to man, and people to people, and receives in return." **EURIPIDES** <note>Euripides (c. 480–406 BCE) was one of the three great tragedians of classical Athens.</note> said that whenever war is being deliberated, no one considers that death is imminent for himself. §. XL. Treaties that are entered into for the sake of commerce <term>commercia; trade agreements between nations</term>, while they sometimes bring benefit to the state, can also undoubtedly be harmful to it at times. Therefore, here too, civil prudence <note>The practical wisdom or "political savvy" required for effective governance.</note> has a role to play. To touch upon at least the first main points, one could debate whether treaties of this kind are beneficial to the state at all. This, however, will be easy to determine only if it is clear whether commerce itself is beneficial to the state. I see that some conclude that trade is, if not useless, at least superfluous, because human nature is content with little, provided we restrain our desires within the boundaries of reason. **BOETHIUS** <note>Anicius Manlius Severinus Boethius (c. 477–524 CE), a philosopher whose work *The Consolation of Philosophy* sought to reconcile faith with reason.</note> says: <margin>(o) Book II, *The Consolation of Philosophy*, prose V, page 32 of the edition by Theodor Sitzmann.</margin> *(o) Nature is content with a few small things; if you try to pressure its satisfaction with superfluities, what you pour in will become either unpleasant or harmful.* From this, some of the ancients also praised the first mortals—whom they imagine lived in the "Golden Age" <note>A mythological period of primordial peace and simplicity, where humanity lived in harmony with nature without trade, laws, or seafaring.</note>—as happy for the very reason that they passed their lives most happily without seafaring and without commerce.

§ XLVII. A prince who intends to enter into a <term>treaty</term> <note>Latin: *foedus*, a formal agreement between nations.</note> with caution must not neglect the safeguards of such agreements: securities, pledges, and hostages. **POLYBIUS** (d) <note>A Greek historian (c. 200–118 BC) who wrote about the rise of the Roman Republic and emphasized practical political wisdom.</note>—after sternly warning that those who rashly entrust themselves to the good faith of others deserve great criticism—adds that those who take timely precautions for themselves as best they can are not to be blamed. ...is the case, I deny. <note>original: *se habere, abnuo*. I have little doubt that anyone who assumes everyone shares these same base morals is being unjust toward many. However, if the enemy of your ally should emerge superior in the war, it is generally agreed that it is better to have a powerful victor as an unreliable friend than as an open enemy. 

Furthermore, it is sometimes very unclear which of the warring parties' cause it is more advantageous to support. Therefore, there is almost no doubt that, at least in such cases, it is beneficial to maintain a middle ground between them. 

Finally, if the warring parties are of unequal strength, the situation becomes equally difficult. For should you join the more powerful side? To make a strong power even more formidable goes against the common consensus of political thinkers. On the other hand, to join the weaker side is the same as voluntarily entangling oneself in their downfall. Therefore, the conclusion we set out to prove follows: sometimes it is to our advantage to join neither of the combatants.

§. II. If the human race had remained in its first state of innocence, there would have been no need for rites, ceremonies, and solemnities. ->### POLITICAL AND MORAL EXERCISES: CONCERNING THAT WHICH IS FITTING<-

It is quite customary to mix human things with divine ones, not only to make the origins of cities more majestic, but also those of nations, families, ranks, and other matters. For this reason, how many fables are told, and how many fabrications exist concerning the origin of illustrious families, the conversion of nations, or the devotion of families to the Christian religion? To what end? *So that they might make the beginnings of things more majestic* <note>original: *ut primordia rerum augustiora faciant*</note>, and to instill in the citizens a sense of veneration toward those who rule over them. 

And even if such fables were mostly invented by foolish flatterers, they are nonetheless shrewdly encouraged thereafter by more skillful men and are counted among the <term>instruments of ruling</term> <note>original: *dominandi instrumenta* — a phrase often used in political philosophy to describe the "tools of power" used by a sovereign to maintain control.</note>. A famous example is provided by those highly celebrated treasures of the French: the *Holy Ampulla of Reims*, the *Shield of Lilies*, and the *Oriflamme* <note>original: *Ampulla Rhemensis, Scutum liliatum, & Auri flamma*. These are the legendary "regalia" of France: the vial of oil used to anoint kings, the fleur-de-lis coat of arms, and the sacred battle-standard.</note>. These things are said to have been sent down from heaven and given by God to King Clovis <note>Clodouaeus (Clovis I), the first King of the Franks to unite the Frankish tribes and convert to Catholicism in the late 5th century.</note>. Yet, they are described with so little appearance of truth—lacking even a trace of probability—that they cannot help but provoke laughter from anyone possessing even moderate judgment. 

Nevertheless, because this popular belief—that some special prerogative comes to the kings of France from these divine gifts—wins great veneration for them, courtiers and those steeped in <term>political mysteries</term> <note>original: *mysteriis politicis* — the "arcana imperii" or secrets of statecraft.</note> do not hesitate to perpetuate it. Most shrewdly also, when France was burning with civil wars, the confederates in the Assembly of Blois in the year 1584 <note>The author refers to the Estates-General at Blois. # CONCERNING THE SOLEMNITIES OF PRINCES #

...[it is said] to have been given to [those] born in Poitiers and to Pontius Paulinus, Bishop of Nola, and is confirmed by Albinus—also known as Alcuin, the tutor of Charlemagne—when he discusses the miracles of the Blessed Martin. To me, certainly, the more prudent men seem to have assigned equal value to the oil of Remigius <note>The sacred oil of Reims, named after Saint Remigius (Saint Rémi), who supposedly received it from a dove for the baptism of Clovis.</note> and the oil of Tours; meanwhile, something had to be invented to deceive the common people.

Nor can I believe that among the learned men of France there is anyone so lacking in all judgment that he seriously persuades himself such a miracle ever occurred at the baptism of Clovis. Hence, if **JEAN-JACQUES CHIFFLET** <note>Jean-Jacques Chifflet (1588–1660) was a Flemish physician and antiquarian who wrote *De Ampulla Remensi* (1651), a skeptical critique of the legend of the Holy Ampulla.</note> wished to teach these people better in his learned commentary on the Ampulla of Reims—in which he laboriously explodes this fiction—he has, in my opinion, "lost both his oil and his labor" <note>original: *operam, mea opinione, oleumque perdidit*. This is a play on a Latin idiom meaning to waste time and effort, punning on the subject of the sacred oil.</note>. 

However, if he wished to free the commoners from this popular error, I doubt he won much favor among the courtiers, whose interest it is that such fictions be believed by the people. Perhaps those historians of France acted more prudently who did not dare to openly call this into doubt, lest this state secret <note>original: *arcanum*</note> be made public; meanwhile, they did not hawk it as true history either, lest they expose themselves to the mockery of the more skilled. 

Instead, they mostly recorded the opinion that sat in their minds by using qualifiers of popular belief, such as *as they say*, *it is reported*, or *rumor has it*. This fact is also observed by the most celebrated man **JOHANN CHRISTOPH BECMANN** <note>A noted German historian and geographer (1641–1717).</note>, appealing to **MICHELE RICCIO**, **JEAN DE SERRES**, **FRANÇOIS DE BEAUCAIRE**, and others.

### §. IX.

However, a different judgment must be passed concerning the external signs and symbols of power and authority. It would be desirable for all citizens to stand by the judgment of reason rather than the representations of the senses; nevertheless, since some allowance must be made for human weaknesses, and a prince cannot otherwise obtain veneration—which is the mother of obedience and loyalty—from the citizens unless he also surrounds himself with an external appearance of majesty, this should not be held against him as a fault. Indeed, if he were to neglect it, he might rightly be judged to be sinning against the rules of prudence <note>The author distinguishes between lying to the people (which is wrong) and using visual splendor to inspire respect (which is a necessary practical skill for a ruler).</note>.

Hence it is not surprising, nor to be blamed, that rulers often claim for themselves a certain pre-eminence <note>original Greek: *ἐξοχὴν* (exochēn)—prominence or superiority.</note> over the citizens, even in the smallest matters. §. XI. It is clear, therefore, from what has been said so far, that a state cannot lack external symbols of authority, and that it is right and lawful for those in command to employ them at times. Among these demonstrations of power and authority, the *solemnities* <term>solemnities: formal, dignified public ceremonies or rites</term> of princes now also hold their place. By this name, we mean nothing other than public acts defined by specific rites and ceremonies suitable for demonstrating the magnificence of the prince and for exciting the veneration of the citizens toward him. These are especially practiced when something has occurred or been performed which it is in the interest of the state for everyone, or at least many, to know. Thus, it is in the interest of the state that the birth of royal children be made known to everyone; likewise, that the marriages of the rulers be clearly established, so that the people are not ignorant of whom they will have as rulers and in what order; and the same must be thought concerning the death of men—

# CONCERNING THE SOLEMNITIES OF PRINCES.

...of men or women who constitute a part of the reigning house <note>Latin: *regnanti domus*. This refers to the immediate royal family or dynasty.</note>. Reason dictates, therefore, that these events be celebrated with public and customary rites <term>rites: established, formal ceremonies, often religious or state-sanctioned</term>, lest those things which everyone ought to know might by chance escape anyone’s notice. The benefits <term>beneficia: favors or blessings bestowed by a superior</term> which God bestows upon citizens through good princes <note>Latin: *principes*. Here used in the broad sense of "rulers" or "sovereigns" rather than just the rank of Prince.</note> are most rightly recalled to memory when those days dawn which first granted these pledges of heaven to mortals. 

Therefore, both piety and the necessity of demonstrating a grateful heart demand that the birthdays of those who rule <note>Latin: *natales imperantium*. The celebration of a monarch's birthday was a central event in the early modern political calendar, linking the ruler’s life to the health of the state.</note> be spent amidst prayers, thanksgivings, and public displays of joy. The same holds true when the august house is increased by new territories or dignities, or when a victory is won over enemies <note>Latin: *victoria ab hostibus reportata*</note>, or some other addition to its happiness has been made. For just as all these things should not remain unknown to the subjects, so it is right that they be celebrated with public signs of joy. 

The same judgment should be held regarding other causes of solemnities, which—as no one is unaware—are various and manifold. In these matters, just as princes rightly present themselves to be seen by their subjects in a certain more majestic form <note>The author argues that grand public appearances are not mere vanity, but a necessary tool of statecraft to inspire awe and respect.</note>, so, while they do those things which contribute both to increasing the love of their subjects and to winning their veneration, they certainly commit nothing that ought to be rebuked.

§. XII. As far as the laws of decorum <term>decorum: the quality of being appropriate or fitting to the circumstances, one's social standing, and the expectations of others</term> are concerned, which must be observed by a prince in these solemn ceremonies, it is first of all necessary that they adapt themselves to the custom of each nation and the opinion of the people, which is based on accepted habits and manners. For decorum consists in the shaping of our acts to the feelings and judgment of others. Yet the feelings and judgments of others vary greatly, and often without any reason—or at least because men have become accustomed to consider this thing beautiful and that thing foul, one thing splendid and magnificent, and another vile and meager. ...I have no doubt at all. Certainly, the rite of crowning and anointing kings, as honorable and splendid as it seems to us, will perhaps be considered ridiculous by other nations, since it is well known that this practice is common only among Christians. Since these things are so, it is the duty of a prince to restrain himself from foreign rites and customs, not only because decorum depends for the most part on the opinion of men, but because subjects are also sometimes offended by foreign institutions.

...they recall to memory. In the consecrations and inaugurations of Christian kings and princes, many ceremonies of this kind occur, which you might designate by the name of Christian decorum <note>original: "decori christiani"</note>. To this I first refer the rite of anointing itself <term>unction: the ritual act of pouring oil upon a person as a sign of divine selection</term>, derived from the Hebrews and passed to the Christians. This was established, if I am not mistaken, so that the ruler might profess through this symbol that his supreme power has been granted to him by God, and that he expects from Him the strength of body and soul to rightly perform the duty imposed upon him. 

Certainly, it was customary from the most ancient times among the peoples of the East to pour oil over their bodies for the sake of refreshment and pleasure; the sweat—undoubtedly brought on by the heat to which they are exposed—prompted them to do this. Just as men freely employ those things which are pleasing to them to demonstrate their affection toward others, and indeed toward God himself, so the custom took hold of anointing with oil those things they wished to be consecrated to God. 

God, however, in His incredible kindness toward mortals, sometimes indulges their weakness; and thus, while He was establishing the church and the commonwealth of the Israelites, He willed that the tabernacle <note>The portable dwelling place for the divine presence described in the Hebrew Bible, used from the time of the Exodus until the building of the Temple of Solomon.</note> and all its vessels should be separated from profane <note>In this context, "profane" refers to common, everyday use rather than something disrespectful.</note> use and hallowed for His worship by anointing. Hence, that which was to be sacred and dedicated to God in a unique way was anointed with oil. Therefore, those anointed...

### CONCERNING THE BEGINNING OF THE SOLEMNITIES.

Z 3

<meta>catchword: For-</meta>

...not only so that he might conform to the accepted custom of anointing kings, but so that he might not perhaps provide an opportunity for others to claim a certain prerogative <note>A special right or privilege, here referring to the Papacy's claim of spiritual superiority over secular monarchs.</note> by being anointed in a different manner. For it is well known that the Roman Pontiffs, in order to exalt themselves above all kings and princes, sought an argument for their higher dignity in the act of anointing itself; they wished that they alone should be anointed on the head, while kings should only be anointed on the arms. This can be proven from the decree of Innocent III <note>Pope Innocent III (reigned 1198–1216), a pivotal figure in defining the medieval papacy's power over secular rulers.</note>, who at the beginning indeed offers other reasons for this distinction regarding a prince, <margin>(n) On sacred anointing, section: *Whence*.</margin> saying: <note>original: "unctio a capite ad brachium est translata, vt princeps ex tunc non ungatur in capite, sed in brachio, seu humero vel armo, in quibus principatus congrue designatur, iuxta illud, quod legitur, factus est principatus super humerum eius &c."</note> *the anointing has been transferred from the head to the arm, so that from then on the prince is not anointed on the head, but on the arm, or shoulder, or bicep, in which the princely rule is appropriately designated—according to that which is read: "the government was placed upon his shoulder," <note>A reference to Isaiah 9:6. The Pope used this to argue that a King's role is physical labor and burden-bearing, whereas the Pope's role is the "head" or intellect.</note> etc. However, the sacramental pouring on the head is reserved for the pontiff, because he represents the person of the Head in the pontifical office.* 

But soon he reveals his mind more clearly, suggesting that this difference in anointing was uniquely devised to signify the prerogative of the pontiff over kings, by hinting: <note>original: "vt ostendatur, quanta sit differentia inter auctoritatem pontificis & principis potestatem."</note> *so that it may be shown how great a difference there is between the authority <term>auctoritas|In Roman and Canon law, 'auctoritas' refers to moral, spiritual, or inherent prestige and right to lead.</term> of the pontiff and the power <term>potestas|Refers to the legal or physical power to command and enforce, often viewed by the Church as secondary to spiritual authority.</term> of the prince.* Yet the Roman prelates failed in this aim, at least regarding the head. For even those kings and princes devoted to the rites of the Roman Church did not hesitate to accept anointing on the head.

### POLITICAL-MORAL EXERCISE ON DECORUM
<note>The Latin title "DE EO QVOD DECET" refers to *decorum*—the philosophical and legal concept of what is fitting, appropriate, or right for a person of a certain status.</note>

The example of the most august King of the Romans, Joseph <note>Joseph I (1678–1711), who was crowned King of the Romans in 1690 and later became Holy Roman Emperor.</note>, still remains in everyone’s memory; it is well established that he was anointed on the neck, on the head, and on both arms. In the anointing of the emperors who have lived through the most recently passed centuries, although there has sometimes been some variation—with some also being anointed on the chest and between the shoulders—they have nevertheless always been anointed on the head as well. In France, it is established that the kings were anointed first on the head, then on the chest, then on the back between the shoulders, and finally on the elbows, with the sign of the cross being made. In England, Thuanus <note>Jacques Auguste de Thou (1553–1617), a renowned French historian and statesman.</note> reports (o) that James <note>King James I of England (James VI of Scotland), whose 1603 coronation combined English and Scottish rites.</note> was anointed on the head, forehead, chest, between the shoulders, and on the arms, hands, and feet, while the queen was anointed only on the head and neck. I omit other examples which Johann Christoph Beckmann <note>Johann Christoph Beckmann (1641–1717) was a notable German historian and academic who wrote extensively on the dignities and titles of European nobility.</note> has collected. (p) 

From these instances arises an observation, which should be placed not in the last position among the rules of decorum: that rites and ceremonies depend indeed on the will of the prince, provided they are suitable to the purpose of the act they accompany and to honorable conduct. Yet sometimes, if certain rites are a symbol and proof of a specific right <term>ius</term> that might be called into question, then they must necessarily be employed, lest a new argument [be used against] our right... <note>The text cuts off here at the end of the page.</note>

...should we wish to offer to another what we must wrest from ourselves. Indeed, today there is hardly a reason for Christian kings to fear the Pope, since he has now learned to trade more cautiously and to extend the limits of his empire through a more subtle reasoning. But in that era, when he exercised his tyranny openly and sought proof of his authority in the variations of anointing <note>The Pope historically claimed that while bishops were anointed on the head, kings should only be anointed on the arm or shoulder to signify their subordination to the Church.</note>, no prince—unless he was very reckless with his own dignity—could allow the anointing on the head to be omitted.

§. XVII. Just as all these rites, which are customarily employed in the inaugurations of princes, are intended to confirm the subjects in their belief that the right to rule has been divinely conferred upon the reigning family, so this very cause requires that women also be taken into account in these acts. Practices in this regard have varied among different peoples, but today among European nations, the custom of likewise crowning and inaugurating high-ranking women prevails. Regarding the Romans <note>Specifically referring to the Roman and Byzantine legal tradition.</note>, this is even less surprising, because they wished the *Augusta* <term>Augusta: The title granted to the Empress, signifying her shared majesty and legal status with the Emperor.</term> to be equal to them in almost all legal rights, as the Emperor Justinian <note>Justinian I (r. 527–565), the Eastern Roman Emperor famous for codifying Roman law.</note> declares on more than one occasion. Hence, it became the custom, especially among the Eastern Emperors, that after they had received the imperial insignia, they themselves would shortly thereafter place the same insignia—consecrated by the hand of the Patriarch <note>The Patriarch of Constantinople, the highest-ranking cleric in the Eastern Church.</note>—upon their wives, as is found in THEOPHANES, CEDRENUS, ZONARAS, GEOR- <note>These are prominent Byzantine chroniclers and historians: Theophanes the Confessor, George Cedrenus, and Joannes Zonaras.</note>

# POLITICAL AND MORAL EXERCISE ON DECORUM
<meta>catchword: palia [likely completing "principalia" or a similar term from the previous page]</meta>

...some [reason] should underlie it, lest anything here be used rashly for mere vain and foolish display, or lest common people persuade themselves it is used so. Meanwhile, I can by no means support those who believe that the greatest mysteries lie hidden in even the smallest things, and who indulge in their interpretations to such an extent that they deserve to be placed in the same category as **WILLIAM DURAND** <note>William Durand (c. 1230–1296) was a prominent French canonist and bishop. His work, the *Rationale Divinorum Officiorum*, is a famous 13th-century treatise that provides elaborate allegorical and symbolic explanations for every detail of the liturgy and church architecture.</note>, who, in his *Rationale of the Divine Offices* <note>original: "rationale suo officiorum diuinorum"</note>, disputes—I know not whether more foolishly or more laboriously—concerning every single rite of the Roman Church, even about the sandals and footwear of bishops, earning nothing but contempt and mockery from those with more sense. For it is enough that nearly a threefold purpose is intended in all these things.

First, so that the divine appointment of princes may be represented to the people, and both the princes and the subjects may be reminded of their duties. To this purpose belong—besides the anointing <note>original: "vnctionem"</note> and coronation, and the ministry of men in holy orders—all the sacred rites, sermons, prayers, and the holy place <note>original: "locus sacer"</note> destined for the inauguration or the celebration of some other more solemn act, and other things of this kind which are usually enumerated in a long series by others. 

The second purpose is that, through magnificent and splendid display, a sense of veneration for those who rule may be instilled in the people; all of these preparations are aimed at securing splendor for the act, and likewise the royal and princely ornaments themselves...

When the cooks received the ox, it was impaled on a square beam of oak; the neck and head were tied with rope, and the rest of the body was secured by iron spikes thrust through holes prepared for that purpose. For three days, the beam was turned by a rotating machine, and the juices <note>original: "liquamen." In this context, it refers to the fatty drippings and juices collected during roasting.</note>—pressed out not by an open flame, but by the heat of glowing coals—were collected in a pan placed beneath. A portion of the roasted ox is usually brought to the royal table, while the rest is left for the multitude to scramble for. <note>The "scramble" (diripiendum) was a common feature of early modern festivals where the public was invited to help themselves to food or wine provided by the sovereign, often resulting in a chaotic and festive display of "plunder."</note>

**MODIUS** (u) records that this same rite was celebrated in Italy when the Emperor **Charles V** was crowned with the diadem by the Pope in Bologna. While more magnificent attire is entirely appropriate for princes, especially during solemn ceremonies, yet a theatrical frivolity in dress cannot fail to diminish their authority; indeed, they sin most gravely against the laws of decorum <term>decorum: the principle of behavior and appearance appropriate to one's station</term> by doing so. What shall I say of Claudius? What of Nero? I wonder greatly how the Roman people were able to endure them for so long. For how could they love those who were more savage than the cruelest beasts? Who could revere those who showed themselves to be more foolish than children in their whole manner of life? ### POLITICAL-MORAL EXERCISES CONCERNING WHAT IS FITTING

However, one must judge whether a person is unkempt due to laziness <note>original: "pigritia"</note> or because they are occupied with other concerns, by considering whether they are diligent in any other matter. If someone wears clothes of little value, yet they are carefully fitted and mended, then—in the judgment of CHIARAMONTI <note>Scipione Chiaramonti (1565–1652) was an Italian philosopher who argued that physical traits and outward habits reveal a person's true character.</note>—if he is poor, he will be considered refined; but if he is rich, he is considered greedy. *For such a man,* he says, *is possessed by a desire for elegance <note>original: "cultus"</note>, yet he avoids expense beneath his dignity and means, which is a mark of greed.* Furthermore, if someone wears clothes that are not cheap but are nevertheless filthy, and is additionally tainted by a dirty body and overall squalor, he signals that he is listless and lazy, rather than greedy. On the contrary, if someone wears clothes that are cheap, worn out, and filthy, he demonstrates that he has reached the furthest degree of greed.

But if anyone should doubt whether the use of low-priced clothing arises from greed or from a contempt for outward elegance, he responds that this can be judged from the rest of the man’s life. Indeed, all these things are correct. And although the common people, through a lack of expertise, may not descend into such specific details, the general indications of character—drawn from dress, outward appearance, and the entire discipline of decorum <note>original: "decori disciplina"; the social and moral code governing behavior and appearance appropriate to one's rank.</note>—are so manifest that one can hardly find anyone who does not make use of them. From this it follows that a prince <note>original: "princeps"; a general term for a ruler or high-ranking leader.</note> must be circumspect in all these matters, if only for this reason: lest he be thought to possess a soft, effeminate mind, [or a]

§. XXIV. Therefore, a prince can err in two directions here: first, through luxury and frivolity, and second, through filth and neglect. In both ways, he incurs the hatred and contempt of his subjects. For luxury and excessive display demonstrate a soft mind <note>original: "animum mollem"; implies a lack of masculine or stoic fortitude</note>, infected by the gravest vices. Filth and the neglect of royal attire demonstrate either a greedy or a lazy man—not to repeat what has already been proven above, that external attire and display are entirely necessary for stirring up the veneration of subjects toward their prince. We shall now add a memorable example of this matter. <term>Jean Bodin</term> (m) <note>Jean Bodin (c. 1530–1596) was a highly influential French jurist and political philosopher whose works on sovereignty shaped modern political science.</note> of Anjou relates that when Louis XI, King of France, had been accepted as an arbiter to settle borders and decide the disputes that stood between the King of Castile and the King of Navarre, he excited laughter and contempt for himself among the Spaniards. For the Spaniards, he says, since they had brought along not only boys but even horses covered in gold clothing and trappings <note>original: "phaleris"; decorative metal plates or ornaments used on horse harnesses</note>, thought it shameful that the King of the French was so filthy in his very cheap attire. *There was no dignity of face in him,* he continues, *no majesty, but [he looked like] a man [suited for] pilgrimages to the saints—*

What **Jean Bodin** <note>Jean Bodin (1530–1596) was a French jurist and political philosopher whose work *The Six Books of the Republic* is a foundational text on sovereignty.</note> relates concerning Louis XI is also confirmed by **Philippe de Commines** <note>Philippe de Commines (1447–1511) was a writer and diplomat who served as a counselor to Louis XI; his *Memoires* are considered a masterpiece of Renaissance history.</note>. This is certainly a most healthy warning, to be observed diligently not only in the meetings of princes, but in all solemn acts.

...as the guiding principle. Therefore, it is a matter of prudence to select, according to the reason of the circumstances, the rituals and external symbols that serve the desired goal; it is also a matter of prudence to temper these so that any suspicion of both luxury and squalor is avoided, ensuring that superfluous things are not employed, nor necessary things lacking. But it is also a matter of prudence, should some defect suddenly arise, to make up for it by taking counsel "as if from the sand" <note>original: "capto velut ex arena consilio"; a Latin idiom referring to making a quick, improvised decision on the spot, much like a gladiator or athlete reacting to the shifting sands of the arena.</note>.

Therefore, the deed of Rudolf of Habsburg, the German Emperor and the most fortunate progenitor of the Austrian house, has always seemed to me worthy of the highest praise for prudence—indeed, even for admiration. For when he was being crowned at Aachen <note>Aquisgranum, or Aachen, was the traditional site for the coronation of German kings and Holy Roman Emperors.</note>, and because the scepter was not present, the estates of the empire <note>The "ordines imperii" or Imperial Estates were the high-ranking nobility and clergy who held the right to participate in the coronation and governance.</note> refused to take the oath of allegiance. He is said to have seized a small cross from the altar and addressed them thus: *“Behold the sign, in which we and the entire world have been redeemed, and let us use this sign in place of the scepter.”* (o) <note>original: "Ecce signum, in quo nos & totus mundus eſt redemtus, & hoc ſigno vtamur loco ſceptri."</note> This was prudent enough. For if Rudolf had postponed the coronation because of the absence of the scepter, he might have given those with ill-will an opportunity to stir up revolution or to devise some scheme to defraud the emperor. If, on the other hand, he had forced the oath from the estates without a scepter and sought to complete the coronation, some might again have fallen into the thought that a great fault or blemish had been cast upon the proceedings...

§. XXVII. Now, we must also explain in a few words what is fitting for subjects regarding the solemnities <note>meaning public ceremonies or state festivals</note> of princes. First, the matter itself teaches us that it is their duty to signify their joy, love, and veneration through certain external symbols and tokens. In this regard, the customs of nations vary no less than the rites which princes use to gain veneration for themselves. Thus, among the Persians of old, it was the custom to strew the roads with wreaths and flowers as a demonstration of public joy. For when the news reached Susa <note>the ancient capital of the Persian Empire</note> that Athens had been captured by Xerxes, HERODOTUS (r) says it affected the Persians remaining there so greatly that *they strewed all the roads with myrtle and burned incense throughout the streets.* Regarding the bridge with which Xerxes joined the Hellespont <note>the narrow strait now known as the Dardanelles, connecting the Aegean Sea to the Sea of Marmara</note> to the mainland, the same HERODOTUS (s) writes: *piling up perfumes of every kind upon the bridges, and strewing the path with myrtle.* BARNABAS BRISSONIUS <note>Barnabé Brisson (1531–1591), a French jurist and scholar whose work "On the Kingdom of the Persians" was a standard reference for Persian history</note>, a most diligent writer on Persian affairs, has collected more on this custom: (t) which [he notes] others...

§. XXVIII. Among the primary ways of signifying joy—both those accepted by the ancients and those still commonly practiced today—public and solemn acclamations must be included. When Saul was declared king of the Hebrews by Samuel, all the people acclaimed him: *Long live the King! 1 Samuel 10:24.* <note>original: "viuat Rex!" This is the first biblical instance of a formal royal acclamation.</note> It is highly probable that this was not omitted when David was anointed at Hebron. Regarding Solomon, it is again explicitly recorded that he was acclaimed: *Long live King Solomon! 1 Kings 1:34, 39.* And of Joash, king of Judah: *2 Kings 11:12. They made him king, and anointed him, and clapping their hands, they said, Long live the King!* <note>The Latin numbering for the Books of Kings often follows the Vulgate system, where 1 and 2 Samuel are called 1 and 2 Kings, and the subsequent books are 3 and 4 Kings. Here, the author refers to the coronation of the young king Joash, protected by the priest Jehoiada.</note> It is clear from both Sacred Scripture and the records of other authors that the same practice prevailed among other peoples of the East. There is also no doubt concerning the Romans, especially since, after the Republic changed <note>A reference to the transition from the Roman Republic to the Empire under the Caesars.</note>, the zeal for flattery grew immensely among this nation. A brilliant example of acclamation, to omit countless others for now, exists in AELIUS LAMPRIDIUS <note>Aelius Lampridius is one of the six fictional or real authors attributed to the *Historia Augusta*, a collection of biographies of Roman Emperors.</note>.

§ XXIX. It is not within the scope of our purpose to review here all those ways of demonstrating joy or love toward a prince. Much less is it my intention to comment at length on panegyric speeches, poems, inscriptions, coins, triumphal arches, and other proofs of reverence and veneration toward a prince of that same kind. At the very least, we will discuss in general terms, according to the rule of our undertaking, what the principle of decorum <term>decori ratio: the logic of what is socially and morally appropriate</term> requires here. Two vices, indeed, must be avoided here: *Cynicism* and *flattery*. Namely, those are guilty of cynicism who refuse to demonstrate their loyalty toward a prince through external symbols of veneration and love, even if these are harmless in themselves—like that famous Diogenes <note>Diogenes the Cynic (c. 412–323 BCE), a Greek philosopher who famously rejected social conventions to live a life of extreme simplicity.</note>, who did not even stand up when Alexander <note>Alexander the Great (356–323 BCE).</note> came to him, and asked nothing else of him than that he not block the warmth of the sun from him with the shadow of his body. If this neglect arises from a certain hatred or contempt for the prince, it deserves the most severe punishment; but if it stems from a false conviction or an error of the intellect, it is all the more worthy of pardon and excuse, because such men violate the rules of decorum rather than those of fundamental honesty. For this reason, the most bitter punishments of the Quakers <note>The Religious Society of Friends (Quakers) were frequently persecuted in the 17th and 18th centuries for refusing to perform "hat-honor" or use formal titles, which they viewed as worldly vanity.</note> by no means...

### 392

->MORAL AND POLITICAL EXERCISES: ON DECORUM<-

...even of speeches, it ought to be banished not only from the literary world, but from the state itself. But let others look for the remedies by which this vice may be countered. We add this: the laws of decorum <term>Decorum: From the Latin "decet," meaning "it is fitting." In political philosophy, this refers to the behavior and speech appropriate to one’s social standing and the occasion.</term> are also violated if someone, even without the intent of flattery, strives to show their devotion to a prince, but does so in a way that is inept and ridiculous—suited more to bringing contempt upon the prince than increasing his glory. Men of this sort, however, are worthy of pity rather than punishment or reward. 

Sometimes, however, they are not allowed to be inept with impunity, specifically when they imprudently heap such praises upon a prince that they seem to reproach him for the very vices of which he is aware—as when the harsh are praised for their clemency, the greedy for their generosity, or the lustful for their chastity. Furthermore, those also sin against this part of decorum who celebrate those acts of princes which are more a source of disgrace to them than an ornament—unless such madness has seized the prince himself that he cannot distinguish the shameful from the honorable, or the unpraiseworthy from the praiseworthy.

<margin>(n) *Epitome of Dio Cassius on Nero*</margin>

How shall a citizen act if he then abstains from that public prayer or thanksgiving? §. XXXVII. [...of our own] manners <note>The text begins with the suffix of the word *nostrorum* (our), continuing from the previous page.</note>, if we compare them with the customs of the ancient Christians, it can be proven without much difficulty that they approach closer to the heathens than to the Christians. The ancient Christians, to be sure, omitted nothing in the **solemnities of princes** <note>Public festivals or state holidays celebrating a monarch's birthday, accession, or victories.</note> that they judged relevant to testifying reverence for the prince. 

But what about our people? They think it a most beautiful and clearly proper thing to revel, to carouse, and to get drunk, provided it is done in honor of the prince. They believe that the solemnities of princes are celebrated not so that they might pour out prayers to God, or give Him thanks for a benefit received, but so that they might obtain the license to commit whatever they wish with impunity. 

They then think they are consulting the honor of the prince most rightly when they strenuously wallow in every kind of vice and pleasure. They do not hesitate to accuse others—who do not do the same, or who perhaps do not approve of this—of neglecting their duty toward princes, or even of outright **high treason** <term>laesae maiestatis: literally "injured majesty," a legal term for crimes against the state or sovereign</term>. 

Wretched mortals! Is the honor of the prince truly served when such things are perpetrated which bring the highest disgrace upon him? [...honor] <note>The text completes the word "dishonor" from the previous page.</note> This is the passage I shall now produce, in which he most clearly describes the manners of the ancient Christians—and, under the name of the pagans, those of the moderns—concerning the **solemnities of princes** <note>Public festivals, such as birthdays or anniversaries of a monarch's reign.</note>; a passage which I therefore deem most worthy of observation: <margin>Apologeticus, chapter 35</margin>

"For this reason, then, Christians are public enemies: because they do not devote to the emperors honors that are empty, false, or rash; because, as people of true religion, they celebrate even the emperors' solemnities with conscience rather than with indulgence. It is a 'grand duty,' forsooth, to bring out braziers and couches into the public, to feast street by street, to transform the city into the appearance of a tavern, to churn the mud with wine, and to run about in mobs toward insults, impudence, and the lures of lust. 

Is public joy thus expressed through public disgrace? Do these things become the solemn days of princes, which do not become other days? Those who observe discipline out of respect for Caesar, abandon it for Caesar’s sake: and the license for bad manners will be called piety; the occasion for luxury will be considered religion. O you who deserve to be condemned!

->§. I.<-

...commends itself with the most plausible appearance <note>The word "proxima" or "maxima" (most likely/greatest) was split across the previous page and this one.</note> to persuade the reader of something. This refers to the psychological anxiety that one's own achievements will be overshadowed when placed side-by-side with the greatness of another.</note> For to anyone who weighs the character of Princes—indeed, of all men—with a little more accuracy, it will be clear that this same disease settles in the minds of many, and from there even erupts into the gravest of vices.

->§. II.<-

It is a maxim of the wise that nothing can be called "great" without comparison. I would add that nothing is rightly understood as "small," "heavy," or "light" without comparison either. Moreover, such is the nature of virtues and vices that they shine forth more brightly through comparison, and are presented to the minds of mortals with a more evident clarity. Nor is it only the habit of the unlearned common people, who are unskilled in civil affairs, to immediately pass judgment on others by establishing a comparison; it is also well-known that the most learned men approve of this same method for pronouncing on the characters of men and, as it were, portraying them. Who is unaware of the practice of Plutarch, <note>Plutarch (c. 46–119 AD) was a Greek philosopher and biographer famous for his "Parallel Lives," which paired famous Greeks with famous Romans to compare their virtues and failures.</note> who in an entire book pits the most outstanding men of Greece and Latium against one another, so that their compared virtues and vices might be brought into the light all the more clearly? <header>ON COMPARISON.</header>
<meta>catchword: Justin-</meta>

Justi]nus <note>The name "Justinus" was split across the previous page and this one. Marcus Junianus Justinus was a 2nd-century Roman historian known for his epitome of Trogus Pompeius’s histories.</note> thought he could not show the character of Philip the father and Alexander the son to his readers more correctly than by setting up a comparison. (b) Alexander the son, he says, succeeded Philip, and was greater than his father in both his virtues and his vices. Their method of conquering was different for each. The former <note>Philip</note> conducted wars through schemes and artifice, while the latter <note>Alexander</note> did so openly. The former rejoiced in deceiving his enemies; the latter in routing them in plain sight. Philip was more prudent in counsel; Alexander more magnificent in spirit. The father could hide his anger and usually even overcome it; for the son, once it had flared up, there was neither delay in vengeance nor any limit to it. Both were excessively fond of wine, but the vices of their drunkenness were different. The father would rush from a banquet against the enemy, join in the fray, and rashly offer himself to dangers; Alexander would vent his rage not on the enemy, but on his own people. Therefore, battles often sent Philip back wounded, while the son frequently left a banquet as a murderer of his friends. The father wanted to reign alongside his friends; the son exercised his rule over his friends. The father preferred to be loved, the son to be feared. The cultivation of literature was similar in both. The father possessed greater shrewdness, while the son possessed greater loyalty. Philip was more moderate in his words and speech, Alexander in his actions. The son’s spirit was both more ready and more honorable in sparing the conquered; the father did not even refrain from violating sacred things. The father was more devoted to frugality, the son to luxury. Among more recent writers, **Benjamin Priolus** (c) <note>Benjamin Priolo (1602–1667), a French historian and diplomat.</note> elegantly compared and contrasted **Cardinal Mazarin** with **Cardinal Richelieu**, just as **Famianus Strada** (d) <note>A Jesuit historian famous for his history of the Dutch Revolt, *De Bello Belgico*.</note> did the **Count of Egmont** with the **Prince of Orange**.

# POLITICAL AND MORAL EXERCISE ON FEAR

Moreover, **RENÉ RAPIN** <note>René Rapin (1621–1687) was a French Jesuit scholar and influential literary critic known for his "comparisons" of classical thinkers.</note> followed the example of Plutarch, for he wrote a very similar work in the French language, (e) in which you may see Cicero compared with Demosthenes, Virgil with Homer, Livy with Thucydides, Aristotle with Plato, and finally Horace with Pindar. But what need is there for more examples in a matter so evident, and about which no one has any doubt?

### §. III.
However, so that we may more correctly discern through comparison whether fear is to be praised or condemned in a prince, it is helpful to look a little more deeply into the nature of comparison itself. Those who strive to penetrate the recesses of the human mind observe that it is only when we compose diverse ideas together—to discover the extent to which they agree with or differ from one another—that we call the process "comparison." In this task, to avoid the errors that creep in everywhere (but especially in comparisons), it is necessary that the subjects we undertake to compare are accurately known and explored by us. One would compare Cicero with Demosthenes in vain unless one had first intimately examined the character, learning, manners, studies, destinies, and eloquence of both...

->OF COMPARISON<-

Dd

...known. <note>original: "tus" — this is the terminal syllable of a word from the previous page, likely "perspectus" (examined) or "cognitus" (known).</note> Above all, however, this must also be carefully weighed: that in a comparison, the idea which is better known to us and is placed as the foundation serves as the **measure**, against which we examine the other, so that we might explore, as it were, the value of that thing and build our judgment upon it. Unless that foundational idea is perfectly clear and correctly established, we can no more promise ourselves true and right judgments than those who attempt to explore the nature or quantity of an object using a deceptive rule or standard. Suppose someone says a prince was braver than **ALEXANDER THE GREAT**, wiser than **SOLOMON**, or holier than **DAVID**: unless the bravery of Alexander, the wisdom of Solomon, and the holiness of David are accurately established in his mind, he should not be thought to have understood what he said. <note>Alexander the Great, Solomon, and David serve here as "ideals" or benchmarks for specific virtues—fortitude, wisdom, and piety—against which all others are measured.</note>

### §. IV.
However, since very few mortals direct the care of their minds toward ensuring that the idea they lay down as the foundation of their judgments—and against which they measure others—is clear and evident, it cannot happen otherwise than that there is a very great diversity both in these "fundamental ideas" (if I may speak thus) and in the judgments themselves. Hence, we are taught daily by experience as our mistress that what one person considers "light," another calls "heavy"; what is called "great" by one appears "small" or "mediocre" to another; and what is judged "honorable" by some, others judge as base...

# THE FORCE OF COMPARISON

In exactly the same way, the matter holds true in morals and civil life. What seems splendid and magnificent to one is base and sordid to another; what seems excellent and glorious to one is seen as contemptible by another, according to the diversity of the idea with which they compare the things to be judged.

This matter gave the <term>Sceptics</term> <note>Sceptics were philosophers who questioned the possibility of certain knowledge, often highlighting how human perception is unreliable and relative.</note> an opening to adopt the opinion that, in this diversity of judgments, nothing certain or stable can be found. ### POLITICAL-MORAL EXERCISE ON FEAR
<margin>420</margin>

**SEXTUS EMPIRICUS** (k) indeed, among the modes for suspending judgment, also includes this: that the nature of relative things (and to this category comparisons belong) cannot be known. *The eighth mode,* he says, *is based on relativity; according to which we conclude that, since all things are relative, we will withhold our assent as to what they are simply and according to their nature.* <note>original: "Octauus est modus ex relatis, secundum quem colligimus, cum omnia sint relata, quaenam sint simpliciter & secundum naturam, nos assensum retenturos."</note> But it is characteristic of these men <note>The Sceptic philosophers.</note> to go further than is fitting. For although some things make the knowledge of matters difficult, they do not immediately or entirely abolish it.

->§. VII.<-

We must now demonstrate how the matters we have discussed thus far relate to our current purpose. Whenever a new <term>prince</term> <note>In this context, *princeps* refers generally to any sovereign ruler or head of state.</note> takes up the reins of government, he is subjected to the judgment of the people. They, by comparing him with his predecessor, easily allow themselves to be led into opinions that will produce either love and veneration, or, on the contrary, hatred and contempt—from which, not infrequently, the safety or ruin of both the ruler and the state depends. If, therefore, when thinking of the predecessor, they hold in their minds the idea of a ruler endowed with all virtues and nearly perfect, they will judge the successor all the more kindly the closer he approaches that idea of a good ruler which they have conceived in their souls; conversely, they will be more prone to contempt to the degree that he falls away from the character of his prede-

...will be more foreign to the predecessor. For the mental image of a predecessor—which is either fresh in the mind, or at least belongs to a ruler whom the people followed with great affection and whose memory has taken deep root—is always present in their thoughts. It serves as a foundation and a yardstick against which they measure the virtues and conduct of all rulers, especially their successors. 

The same principle applies if one succeeds a hated ruler or a tyrant. In that case, the further the successor moves away from the image of his predecessor, the more he will be welcomed; however, the more he approaches that predecessor's example, the more he will be loathed. 

Thus, the people do not judge rulers by one and the same standard, nor is there any constant and eternal rule to be found to which rulers might conform themselves. Therefore, nothing else remains for a ruler who desires to win the love of the people but to investigate what kind of "image of a good ruler" dwells in their minds—specifically, which of his predecessors they valued most—so that he may model his own character and actions after that example.

->§. VIII.<-

However, a very great difficulty sometimes arises here: experience teaches us that the public not infrequently loves a ruler's vices, while conversely hating his virtues. <note>The Latin header "DE METU" translates to "On Fear," though the text continues the previous section’s theme of comparison and reputation.</note>

Similarity in external traits—provided other things correspond reasonably well—carries great weight; however, it is ultimately stripped of all force and effectiveness if a glaring difference in virtues and character is openly perceived. Hence **AELIUS SPARTIANUS** <note>A Roman historian traditionally credited as one of the authors of the *Historia Augusta*.</note> correctly adds: *But hope greatly deceived him (Emperor Severus). For the state was deprived of one by parricide, and of the other by his own character; and that sacred name (of the Antonines) did not remain well in either of them for long.* <note>original: "Sed illum (Severum imperatorem) multum spes fefellit. Nam unum parricidium, alterum sui mores reipublicae inuiderunt: sanctumque illud nomen (Antoninorum) in nullo diu bene mansit." Emperor Septimius Severus hoped his sons Caracalla and Geta would rule like the great Antonine emperors, but Caracalla murdered his brother Geta (the "parricide") and his own cruelty ruined the family's reputation.</note>

§. IX. Since these things are so, a wise prince is rightly judged to have just cause to be anxious about the comparison he may perhaps undergo among the common people. It should be clear to everyone from what has been said so far that this comparison—which can nevertheless bring the greatest contempt upon a prince—relies for the most part on a slippery, uncertain, and sometimes even foolish foundation. One person measures a good prince by his external appearance, another by his generosity, another by his leniency, and another by the victories he has won over enemies. How difficult it is, therefore, to obtain the praise of being a good prince from everyone! Suppose a prince is just, brave, and wise: let him succeed a ruler who was accustomed to soothing the minds of the people with his outward physical appearance, the splendid pomp of his court, public games, and a nearly intolerable leniency; if the successor is not like him in all these things, the goodwill of the people will be almost finished, [and] the present state of affairs...

### ON COMPARISON

NICOLAVS MACHIAVELLVS <note>Niccolò Machiavelli (1469–1527), the Italian diplomat and philosopher famous for his treatise *The Prince*, which often explored the pragmatic—and sometimes amoral—necessities of power.</note> teaches (l) that a prince must, above all, avoid those things which might make him hated and despised. However, HERMANNVS CONRINGIVS <note>Hermann Conring (1606–1681), a German physician and political scientist who wrote extensive commentaries on Machiavelli from a more moralistic and legalistic perspective.</note> rightly adds: (m) "But in truth, he will not be able to turn away (contempt and hatred of himself) in any other way unless he is endowed with a civic virtue <term>virtus: in this context, the specific qualities of leadership and character required of a citizen-ruler.</term> that is not feigned, but true—or at least possessed of it for the most part."

Certainly, no one can gain the love of good and wise men in any other way; although even corrupt princes are usually dear to the wicked, and those who have learned to fake virtue are dear to the unrefined and inexperienced. This, without doubt, is the very core of all **Machiavellian folly**: the belief that feigned and simulated virtue has the same efficacy as that which is true and unmasked. In this, however, he erred most shamefully. For no matter how great a display simulated virtue casts before the eyes and minds of subjects, their wickedness eventually shines through; once their hypocrisy is betrayed, it draws upon them a greater hatred and a deeper contempt from all those of sounder judgment.

The same Machiavelli is also mistaken when he thinks it is sufficient for a prince's security if he merely avoids hatred and contempt. For, in addition, the love and goodwill of the subjects must be gained—something which a ruler who has merely avoided their hatred and contempt cannot immediately promise himself. Therefore, CONRINGIVS rightly adds: *Howsoever...*

->§. XIV.<-

Therefore, a prince should take care of his own estimation and fame, but not so much for his own sake as for the sake of his subjects and the state; and this should be done not with a feigned appearance of virtue, but with true and genuine virtue <term>virtus: refers here to the moral excellence and strength of character required for leadership.</term>. §. XVI. Yet, before we depart from this topic, we must not overlook that since laziness is usually accompanied by indulgence and the overlooking of crimes, such princes are not infrequently commended as merciful and kind by the corrupted judgments of mortals on this account. This state of affairs brings great hatred—indeed, it brings ruin—upon their successors if they attempt to correct the deep-rooted vices of the citizens with sharper punishments, as the common people compare them unfairly with their previous masters. # §. XVIII.

**Suspicion**, therefore, although it is sometimes joined with the **fear of comparison**, nevertheless differs from it. For by suspicion, we mean a process of reasoning based on signs—sometimes slight and very uncertain—concerning another person's disposition toward us, with a determination toward the worse side <note>original: "cum determinatione in partem deteriorem." This refers to a cognitive bias where one assumes the worst possible motive or outcome without sufficient evidence.</note>. 

For those who immediately judge, from any gesture or word, that others are hostile to them, do not wish them well, envy their glory, or stand in the way of their interests—even though they lack a suitable argument to prove this—are called **suspicious**. This indeed occurs most often in those who are themselves of a malevolent mind toward everyone else, since it is a condition of our mind that we measure others by our own nature, and we are quite prone to judging that others are endowed with the same character <note>original: "moribus"</note> as ourselves. 

But the **fear of comparison** can certainly exist in those who are otherwise not so suspicious. For indeed, as we shall soon say, it affects even prudent and noble <note>original: "generosos"</note> men who do not indulge in suspicions, yet are concerned for their reputation <note>original: "existimatione"</note> when they are shown by certain and by no means empty arguments that the judgments of the common people are wavering and are being turned in an unfavorable direction by an unfair comparison. 

Added to this is that suspicion, if accurately considered, is an effect of **hatred**. This is what the Apostle <note>A reference to St. Paul. The quote is from 1 Corinthians 13:5, where he describes the nature of "charity" or "love" (agape).</note> also implies, teaching that suspicion cannot coexist with love: *love [thinks no] evil* <note>original Greek: "ἡ ἀγάπη τὸ κακὸν" (hē agapē to kakon). The author is quoting the New Testament to show that love and suspicion are opposites.</note>

### §. XIX. 

Finally, a most distinguished <note>original: "honestissima," which can mean most honorable or most respectable. Here, it refers to the high social standing of the individuals involved.</note> form of the **fear of comparison** appears in those who, led by a desire for glory and praise, conform themselves to the outward appearance of virtue. These men usually set before themselves great figures of the past whom they desire—if not to surpass—at least to equal. In this way, Alexander the Great and Julius Caesar are said to have emulated Hercules. They themselves leave behind an example that others strive to approach; the more sharply a man is driven by the stings of vain ambition, the more closely he tries to reach that standard. 

Consequently, if they believe they surpass or equal certain others in virtue or glory—or at least wish to be seen as doing so—they cannot help but find it most grievous to be drawn into a comparison where they might emerge as inferiors. Truly, these men, whose minds have been touched by the poison of ambition, do everything within their power to increase their glory, power, and authority. Indeed, as Cicero says, (x) they neglect all that is right and honorable as long as they may attain power. Nevertheless, because they usually rely on the great merit of their famous deeds and do not believe that anyone can easily be preferred over them, <margin>Compare the examples in Brockmand’s *Historical Specimens of Ethics*, p. 541 (u)</margin> <margin>Cicero, *On Duties*, Book III (x)</margin>

do not so easily conceive a **fear of comparison** in their minds. ### §. XX. 

You might say that in these cases, the **fear of comparison** comes very close to **emulation** <term>aemulatio: a competitive desire to equal or excel another, often used by Latin moralists to describe a specific type of rivalry</term>. I do not deny this, provided it is also observed that there is nonetheless a great difference between **emulation** and the **fear of comparison**. 

For **emulation** has no place except among the living: but the **fear of comparison** pertains to predecessors, even if they are now dead, as well as to successors. **Emulation** is moved by the excellence of the person to whom we think it would be shameful and unworthy to yield in a particular matter: but the **fear of comparison** is also excited by the judgments of others, when they compare us with someone else, whether that person is dead or still living. 

Finally, **emulation** is either the daughter or the companion of **ambition** <term>ambitio: in a Latin moral context, this often implies an excessive or "empty" thirst for honor (vanity) rather than just a drive for success</term>, and thus it is always to be regarded as a vice. The **fear of comparison** is for the most part blameworthy; yet sometimes, if a concern for one's reputation <note>original: "existimationis cura"</note> proceeds from a true love of the people, it is to be praised as the fruit of true and genuine **prudence** <term>prudentia: the virtue of practical wisdom, or the ability to discern the right course of action</term>.

### §. XXI. 

This doubt could seem to some people to be either plainly false or incorrect: the idea that **emulation**—as either the daughter or the companion of **ambition**—is always rooted in vice. Indeed, the praise with which **emulation** is daily adorned would seem to prove that not all forms of it should be utterly rejected or condemned. Among many others, **Johann Heinrich Boeclerus** <note>Johann Heinrich Boecler (1611–1672) was a prominent German historian and professor of eloquence, known for his commentaries on classical texts.</note> expresses a different view on this matter. He confirms that famous line by **Velleius Paterculus** <note>A Roman historian (c. 19 BC – c. AD 31) who wrote a compendium of Roman history.</note>: *emulation nourishes genius* <note>original: "alit aemulatio ingenia"</note>, and he laboriously explains the distinction between good and wicked **emulation**. (y)

*Emulation,* he says, *is either good and joined with virtue—specifically when admiration kindles imitation—or it is wicked and joined with envy, which our author likewise touches upon. The former, being effective, is desirable; the latter we believe should be left to the profane <note>Those "outside the temple," or the uninitiated/unrefined.</note>, who do not have time to ask in what manner someone has attained learning, but only how much. God usually wills the former to reach great heights, but only occasionally permits the latter to do so. The former is accompanied by serious honor and the judicious use of studies; the latter is almost always accompanied by pomp and empty splendor. The former tends to be found near the peak of studies, the latter near their decline. Indeed, the fame of studies is lowered not by emulation and imitation, but by affectation, the premise <note>original: ὑπόθεσιν (hypothesin). Boecler uses the Greek term to refer to the underlying basis or theme of Velleius’s description.</note> of which Velleius has brilliantly described. Truly, just as that praiseworthy emulation [springs] entirely from virtue and a zeal for the public good...*

<note>Aristotle defines emulation as: "Emulation is a certain pain at the apparent presence of honorable goods, which it is possible for one to acquire, among those similar in nature; not because they belong to another, but because they do not also belong to oneself." (Original Greek: ζῆλός ἐστι λύπη τις ἐπὶ φαινομένῃ παρουσίᾳ ἀγαθῶν ἐντίμων καὶ ἐνδεχομένων αὐτῷ λαβεῖν περὶ τοῖς ὁμοίοις τῇ φύσει, οὐχ᾽ ὅτι ἄλλῳ, ἀλλ᾽ ὅτι οὐχὶ καὶ αὐτῷ ἐστί.)</note>

**Emulation** is a certain distress caused by the apparent presence of honorable goods—of the sort that it is possible for one to acquire for oneself—among those who are our equals by nature. This distress arises not because these goods belong to another, but because they do not also belong to oneself. Or, what is much the same: it is a distress concerning goods which we lack, arising from the admiration of those goods in others, and accordingly joined with the desire of either surpassing others or acquiring the same things for oneself.
