### EXERCISE IN POLITICAL MORALITY ON FEAR ###

...rightly commands us to cast out all emulation. To say that **God** wills men to reach high things through **emulation** can hardly be said without impiety. Does **God** really favor the **ambition** of men? These are the fruits of **pagan philosophy** <note>original: *philosophiae ethnicae*; the author refers to Classical Greek and Roman thought which often celebrated "agon" or competition, contrasting it with Christian humility</note>. Indeed, even if emulation accompanies the most serious pursuit of honor or the wise application of one's studies, it does not for that reason cease to be a vice. Both the peak and the decline of studies can be joined with wicked emulation: **ambition** reigns everywhere, among the learned and the barbarians alike.

Finally, his <note>referring again to Boecler</note> addition—that "good" emulation proceeds from **virtue** and a zeal for the public good—cannot be admitted either. The **virtue** which emulation produces, or which is joined with it, is not virtue at all, but **ambition**. Nor does he truly desire to consult the **public good** <note>original: *publicum bonum*</note> who, led by emulation, promotes the advantages of the **state** <note>original: *reipublicae*</note>; rather, he seeks to satisfy his own greed for status. Why, then, could virtue, or the study of the public good, not exist without emulation?

§. XXII. But, they say, talents will grow sluggish in the **schools**, and the **virtue** of soldiers will languish on the battlefield, unless they are excited by emulation. The same things can be said in favor of the **fear of comparison** <note>original: *metus comparationis*; the anxiety caused by being measured against others</note>. For, although these two things differ, we have conceded that they agree in many respects. Therefore, the arguments we have raised against **emulation** must be understood as being directed also against the <term>fear of comparison</term> <note>the specific psychological dread of being found inferior to a peer during a public evaluation</note>, insofar as it aligns with emulation.

<meta>This page continues the author's critique of emulation (competitive rivalry) as a pedagogical tool. # OF COMPARISON #

Indeed, you may see the use of **emulation** <note>original: *aemulatio*; here meaning the competitive drive to surpass others in status or rank</note> in acquiring **learning** <note>original: *eruditio*</note> so highly praised that there is hardly any school among Christians that this plague has not infected. The diligence of boys is provoked not only by rewards and punishments, but especially by granting a more honorable rank to the one who has surpassed another.

In this way, by deliberate effort, the **ambition** <note>original: *ambitio*; the pursuit of honor and social standing</note> lurking in the hearts of mortals is excited; and already at a tender age, boys become accustomed to not being able to endure an equal or a superior. Those who make progress when incited by these goads are praised and adorned with great eulogies.

Once they have become adults, they retain these same habits: hence come ferocity, pride, and the lust for contradicting and conquering; hence come the lawsuits and controversies by which either the **church** or the **state** <note>original: *ecclesia aut respublica*</note> is miserably torn apart, along with an infinite army of evils. We see this, and we deplore it; yet there is hardly anyone who has rightly investigated the source and primary origin of this evil, or who has seriously thought to bring a remedy.

To be sure, laziness must be shaken off and talents must be awakened—I admit this. But that this must be done by injecting **emulation** into very tender minds, that I truly deny. This is just as if someone were to deliberately run into **Scylla** <note>In Greek mythology, Scylla and Charybdis were two sea monsters on opposite sides of a narrow strait; "falling into Scylla to avoid Charybdis" is a classic idiom for escaping one danger only to fall into a worse one</note>, or cast others into it, simply to avoid **Charybdis**. And yet, we behave this way in correcting most vices: we use contrary vices, often far more destructive, as remedies for them...

<meta>This page continues the author’s argument against using "emulation" or competitive rivalry as a teaching tool. Having previously compared it to the danger of steering into a whirlpool to avoid a rock, the author now explains why people mistakenly praise this vice and offers "piety" as the true alternative.</meta>

->### POLITICAL-MORAL EXERCISES ON FEAR ###<-

...let us oppose. Nor is it surprising, since those who have strayed from the royal road of **Christian virtue** <note>original: *christiana virtus*; the author refers to the balanced path of moral excellence according to faith</note> can hardly behave otherwise, given the great corruption of our human nature. They see the disadvantages of a particular **vice** <note>original: *vitium*</note>; they realize that this vice can somehow be avoided by fleeing to its opposite vice. They seize upon this second vice because they lack any other way to escape their current situation. And because it often happens that more serious troubles are suppressed for a time, they even congratulate themselves, as if they had performed a brilliant deed. This is the source of that common praise for **emulation** <note>original: *aemulatio*; a competitive drive to outdo others</note>.

But these miserable people do not notice that subtler vices are the most dangerous. It may happen that the troubles of one vice are avoided for a time, only for the far greater damages of another vice—the one opposite to the first—to burst forth; these damages eventually reject all medicine. Therefore, let the minds of boys be imbued with true **piety** <note>original: *pietas*; a sense of devotion and duty toward God</note>: this will shake off laziness and lethargy, and it will keep them safe from the poison of **ambition** <note>original: *ambitio*</note> and other vices.

The same reasoning applies to other men, whom we think must be incited by competition to fulfill the requirements of their **duty** <note>original: *officium*; a person's social or professional responsibility</note>. ### §. XXIV. ###

Philosophers, for their part, are also accustomed to speak of envy in such a way that they seem to admit no distinction between it and the fear of comparison. **ARISTOTLE** (k) says that *those who are placed in an illustrious position and endowed with prosperous fortune are envious,* <note>original: "εἰ μεγάλα πράττοντες καὶ εὐτυχοῦντες" — those doing great things and being fortunate</note> *and they feel envy in those matters from which they seek glory.* By this very statement, he seems to suggest that the envious are those who cannot bear for others to be preferred over themselves once a comparison is established. -># OF COMPARISON #<-

For [unequals] could not be compared with one another; but **envy** <note>original: *inuidia*</note> holds sway among equals and unequals alike. The <term>fear of comparison</term> <note>original: *metus comparationis*; an anxiety about how one’s status is perceived relative to another.</note> looks toward the judgments of others. Indeed, it is such that for one who fears comparison, it would otherwise be of no consequence how great the glory or virtue of another might be, as long as nothing was taken away from their own **reputation** <note>original: *existimatio*</note> by it—that is, as long as their own virtue or glory, when compared with the former in the judgment of the public, did not appear inferior or lesser.

But the envious person does not care for the judgments of a third party; they are tormented, tortured, and indignant that another possesses certain goods which they believe should more rightly be possessed by themselves. From this, a further distinction comes to light: the fear of comparison is preoccupied with preserving **fame** and reputation, whereas all the goods of another person, of whatever kind they may be, are displeasing to the envious man: wealth, houses, lands, a great number of noble friends, physical beauty, honor, glory, and finally even **virtue** <note>original: *virtus*; here meaning moral excellence or skill.</note> itself.

Furthermore, envy is usually extinguished by the death of the person envied; for the envious person rejoices if the one whose presence caused them such distress and pain is removed from their sight. Yet the fear of comparison finds its place most of all when the living are compared with the dead. This is even more the case because the virtues of the dead are sometimes only commemorated while their **faults** <note>original: *vitia*; literally "vices" or defects.</note> are passed over, whereas the faults of the living, no less than their virtues, [dwell] in the minds... <note>The sentence ends abruptly as the catchword "ocu-" (likely *oculis*, "eyes") leads to the next page.</note>

this is not to be thought. Or does he understand divine providence itself? It must be understood—or at least implied—when we use the word "fortune," unless we wish to designate by this term something that is either impious <note>original: *impium*; to suggest that events happen without God's will was considered a religious offense.</note> or foolish. The Stoics <note>A school of ancient Greek philosophy that taught that the path to happiness is found in accepting the present moment and not allowing oneself to be controlled by the desire for pleasure or the fear of pain.</note>, as mentioned elsewhere, observe three stages in the passions: *inclination*, *assent*—or *synkatathesis* <note>original Greek: "συγκατάθεσιν" (synkatathesis); the internal "yes" or agreement the mind gives to a feeling or thought.</note>—and *impulse*—or *horme* <note>original Greek: "ὁρμὴν" (hormen); the active drive or "setting out" toward an object of desire or away from an object of fear.</note>. ### THE USES OF COMPARISON

->[Gg 3]<-

<meta>catchword: Is,</meta>

...[to be condemned] and obscured daily, will be cursed by anyone who has not entirely cast off every sense of duty and honor. For it is well established that others are harmed no less in their reputation and standing than in their property and body. To harm an innocent person in any way is a crime—as reason teaches all people, and as even the most <term>barbarian nations</term><note>The author uses "barbarian" in the classical sense to refer to non-Roman or non-European cultures, suggesting that the rule of not harming the innocent is a universal human law.</note> do not deny. 

Nor are these behaviors found only among princes or those handling civil affairs. They reign everywhere. The **fear of comparison** also frequently agitates the learned, and those who wish to appear wise, driving them toward any sort of foul and unworthy conduct. For just as nothing is more frequent among them than envy and rivalry—which almost never fail to accompany the fear of comparison—so too a more abundant crop of detractions and slanders flourishes nowhere more than in the <term>**Republic of Letters**<note>original: "eruditorum republica". This refers to the international community of scholars and intellectuals who corresponded and shared knowledge across borders during the Renaissance and Enlightenment.</note></term>.

#### §. XXX. The third effect is foolish imitation.

For there is no imitation without comparison. Whenever we see others doing something we deem worthy of praise, or perceive them to be endowed with manners and gestures that perhaps please us, we realize—once a comparison has been made—that we have not yet done those things or been endowed with those manners. When we strive to become like them in these matters by doing the same things and expressing similar manners and gestures, then we are said to imitate them.

# POLITICAL AND MORAL EXERCISE ON FEAR

The person whom we imitate is like a model, as it were; the closer people approach this model, the more perfect they consider themselves to be as imitators. From this, it is clear that a desire to acquire greater perfection is always joined to imitation. This confirms the opinion of certain philosophers that imitation proceeds from <term>self-love<note>original: "philautia". In classical philosophy, this refers to a natural regard for oneself, which here is argued to be the engine that drives humans to improve by copying those they admire.</note></term> and is, as it were, innate to all human beings. 

If, therefore, that which pleases us—and which we strive to express through our actions, character, and gestures—is truly good and worthy of praise, and is not repugnant to our own nature or disposition, then this type of imitation is called good and commendable. On the other hand, if we should imitate vices, or if we seek a certain excellence and glory in foolish and ridiculous things, or if the thing being imitated is suited to another’s nature and disposition but not to our own, who would praise this? Who would not instead declare that the famous line of **HORACE** applies to such a person:

> O slavish herd of imitators!

However, the learned prefer to call this vice <term>unhealthy affectation<note>original: "κακοζηλίαν" (kakozēlian). A Greek term used in rhetoric and ethics to describe a "faulty zeal" or a perverse, tasteless imitation of a model's flaws rather than their virtues.</note></term> rather than true imitation. One is guilty of this kind of vice:

> —if anyone, with a fierce look, bare feet,
> And a skimpy toga, should try to simulate **Cato** by way of the weaver,

<margin>(u) Book 2, Epistle 19.</margin>

This is what I have said: there is always an **antipathy** <note>original: *antipathiam*; an instinctive or natural aversion between things or people.</note> between the good and the wicked. Just as it largely originates from the **fear of comparison** <note>original: *comparatinois metu*</note>, so too does it in turn increase that same fear and drive men toward more serious crimes.

§. XXXII. **TACITUS** <note>Publius Cornelius Tacitus, a Roman historian known for his dark psychological portraits of emperors.</note> notes a singular effect of this fear in Tiberius: that he abstained from attending public spectacles. For those who fear comparison sometimes seek retreats and hiding places, and they remove themselves from the sight of men. First, they hope that by this very act, they will snatch away from the people the opportunity to form a comparison. For presence, just as it moves the senses, also excites judgments and comparisons—especially in more solemn ceremonies, where people are accustomed to observing a prince's gestures, clothing, and other details more curiously. Next, many adopt the opinion that their authority and the respect they receive are increased the more rarely they are seen.

Hence arises a new reason for hiding oneself. In this matter, as in many others, **Philip II, King of Spain**, is compared with Tiberius. Both had a somber, crafty, and suspicious nature. Both had inherited a predecessor who was affable, humane, magnificent, and possessed of a graceful physical presence—someone fit to win the hearts of the people by their mere presence alone. # ON THE FEAR OF COMPARISON

...in that person with whom he is compared, should he discover qualities which he himself is unable to express or imitate, *a virtuous man strives to compensate for this with other virtues.* Nature has quite often denied honest and upright men certain qualities: physical beauty, graceful gestures, affability, eloquence, and other things by which the common people are usually won over. For although some of these things may seem attainable through practice, nature nevertheless <term>plays the dominant role in the whole account<note>original: *utramque facit paginam*. A Latin idiom literally meaning "makes both pages," referring to the two sides of a ledger; it implies that nature is the deciding factor in both the beginning and the end of one's abilities.</note></term>.

Indeed, if anyone should desire to adopt manners and gestures that are repugnant to his nature, a ridiculous <term>affectation<note>original: *affectatio*. This refers to a labored or artificial manner of behaving, often seen in the early modern period as a sign of vanity or lack of self-knowledge.</note></term> eventually arises from it. It is therefore the mark of a wise man to let these things go and, conversely, to make use of his own strengths; he should not crave what he sees has been denied to him, but should all the more diligently cultivate those virtues to which the path is closed to no one.

These are the principal fruits—though not all of them—of that fear which we have called devoid of vice. From these it is at least certain that, through virtue, the nature of man can be turned toward the good, so that we may hope for an increase in our happiness; but if <term>cultivation<note>original: *cultura*. Similar to the "culture" of a field (agriculture), this refers to the "tilling" of the mind and soul through education, discipline, and habit.</note></term> is not applied, human misery and calamity tend to increase.

In this matter, all roles are to be attributed to **God**; it is enough for a human being if he does not resist or struggle, and if he diligently avoids those things which can hinder the efficacy of the means established by God himself. It escapes no one what the power of **education**, habit, and the daily social intercourse we have with others is, whether toward strengthening or breaking our vices. ...they promised. For without a doubt, the professors of this art of alchemy deceive one another, since, being conscious of their own ignorance, they admire those who have said anything of this kind that seems superior to their own knowledge. To these men, since the truth they seek is never available, they "see the day" <note>original: "diem cernunt"; a Latin idiom meaning to consume time or wait in vain for a specific outcome.</note> and exhaust their resources. These same people conceal their falsehood with words, so that finally, through a <term>sophistical</term> <note>Meaning deceptive or based on a false appearance of truth.</note> transmutation, they forge what does not exist in the nature of things—namely, true gold or silver. Sometimes their condemned and damnable audacity proceeds so far that they strike the characters of public coinage in untrustworthy metals, so that they might elude the faithful eyes of the public and the ignorant commoners, who are otherwise unacquainted with the alchemical fire of the furnace. Wishing, therefore, these practices to be banished for all time, we decree by this edictal constitution that whoever shall have made gold or silver of this sort, or shall have ordered it to be made, etc., shall be compelled to pay into the public treasury, as a penalty to be distributed to the poor, an amount of true gold or silver of the same weight as the alchemical product, etc.

The <term>pontiff</term> <note>Referring to the Pope.</note>, therefore, assuming that the <term>transmutation</term> <note>The alchemical process of changing one metal into another, specifically base metals into gold.</note> of metals is impossible, and that all those who profess this art are close to being impostors, decreed such a thing against alchemists. For this reason, alchemy is also specifically forbidden to <term>clerics</term> <note>Members of the clergy or ordained priests.</note> in that same decree; and if the offenders are clerics, they shall, beyond the aforementioned penalties, be deprived of the <term>benefices</term> <note>A Church office that provides an income to the holder.</note> they hold, and shall be rendered utterly ineligible to hold them in the future.

...[is the] wretched lot of most of those who profess it. It happens to all too many that, having turned their estates, goods, and entire inheritances into ash and smoke, while they softly promise themselves the rewards of long labor, the golden offspring yet to be born, and perpetual health with renewed youth, and having consumed much time and expense, they then for the first time find themselves old, aged, in rags, hungry, always smelling of sulfur, and filthy with black soot among the coals. ...the school of chemists professes to know something. <note>This completes the thought from the previous page: "the practitioners of the chemical art..."</note> From this point, the antagonists of the alchemists rattle on about "species" and "forms," <note>In Aristotelian philosophy, "form" is the essential nature or "soul" of an object, while "species" defines its category. They persuade themselves of such sanctity in these metaphysical canons that anyone who does not consider it a religious duty to doubt them must be immediately regarded as an atheist. 

But in truth, a more sound physics <note>A reference to the "New Science" or mechanical philosophy of the 17th century, which began to replace abstract Aristotelian logic with physical, corpuscular explanations of matter.</note> long ago outlawed these forms and species, along with the whole chorus of words signifying nothing, and granted them an honorable seat in the imaginary spaces of the world. Thus, there is no reason for a practitioner of alchemy to allow himself to be troubled by this point. 

ATHANASIUS KIRCHER <note>Athanasius Kircher (1602–1680) was a famous Jesuit polymath and author of *Mundus Subterraneus*, where he famously attacked the claims of alchemists as fraudulent or impossible.</note> thinks he will prostrate the forces of the alchemists with a single blow when he calculates his arguments as follows: if that *metamorphosis* <note>original: *metamorphosis* (Greek: μεταμόρφωσις), meaning a complete change of form or nature.</note> can happen in metals, it should also be possible in the animal and vegetable kingdoms. For example, if a powder made from wormwood <note>original: *absynthium*</note> were cast upon a dry and dead stalk of wormwood, by the same reasoning, it would revive it into a living plant. The same should be said of a powder made from a burned animal and cast upon the corpse of the same or another animal. <note>This refers to "palingenesis," the idea that a plant or animal could be regenerated from its own ashes, a common topic of debate in 17th-century chemistry.</note> Likewise, if a drop of wine distilled seven times or more were poured into a vat of water, the water would turn into wine. ...that the nature of subjects is not the same, nor does nature operate in the same way in all things. The "proximate common matter" <note>original: *materiam metallorum proximam communem*. In Scholastic philosophy, "proximate matter" is the immediate substance from which a specific thing is formed, as opposed to "prime matter," which is the universal substrate of all things.</note> of metals is of one kind, but it is not the same for plants and animals. Metals are mixed from a few similar parts and have a simpler texture; <note>The word "texture" here refers to the internal arrangement of particles or "corpuscles," a key concept in 17th-century mechanical philosophy which suggested that the properties of matter depend on how its smallest parts are fitted together.</note> plants and animals consist of so many dissimilar parts and are produced in a plainly different way. Mindful of my intended purpose, I omit the rest.

However, if my own opinion is to be set forth, I believe that it is argued here in vain without experience. <note>original: *experientia*. In this context, it refers to empirical observation and experimental results rather than just personal life experience.</note> If this is not provided, it is not easy to either affirm or deny whether the transmutation of metals is possible. For the nature and essence of all things—and thus also of metals—is unknown to us. We learn their operations and properties through experience, but we remain ignorant of their true nature. Whatever philosophers devise concerning the essence of things are merely conjectures and nothing more; they are rejected with the same ease with which they are put forward.

JEAN LE CLERC <note>Jean Le Clerc (1657–1736), also known by his Latin name Joannes Clericus, was a prominent Genevan man of letters and a theologian. §. IX. But, before we look at experimental evidence, <note>original: *experientia*. In the 17th century, this term referred both to personal experience and the emerging concept of scientific experimentation.</note> something must be said about the obscurity that alchemists affect, because by it they make the whole art suspect to many. For it is not uncommon among the race of scholars to commend trifles and more-than-childish inventions with grand and "foot-and-a-half-long" <note>original: *sesquipedalibus*. This is a classical allusion to Horace, referring to overly long, pompous words used to impress others.</note> words, and to cover them with these wrappings, so that the more ignorant might believe great mysteries lie hidden beneath them. Thus in the writings of alchemists you see nothing but riddles, <note>original: *aenigmata*</note> of the **green lion**, <note>A common symbol in alchemy often representing vitriol or a strong acid capable of dissolving gold.</note> of the **fugitive stag**, <note>Often symbolizes mercury or the volatile spirit that flees the heat of the fire.</note> of the **flying eagle**, of the **dancing fool**, of the **dragon devouring its own tail**, <note>The Ouroboros, an ancient symbol of the cyclical nature of the universe and the "All is One" philosophy.</note> of the **bloated toad**, of the **crow's head**, <note>The *caput corvi* or *nigredo* stage, representing the initial blackening or putrefaction of the matter.</note> and of that **black blacker than black**, of the **seal of Hermes**, of the **clay of wisdom**, and others of this kind which are almost innumerable.

When asked what the philosopher's stone might be, Brother **ELIAS OF ASSISI** <note>Likely referring to Elias of Cortona (c. 1180–1253), a high-ranking Franciscan and early associate of St. Francis who was later associated with alchemical legends.</note> answers: *Our stone is from the four elements; the rich have it as much as the poor; it is found everywhere and is likened to all things; it is composed of soul, body, and spirit, and is converted from nature into nature, up to the final degree of its perfection.* 

But **ARNOLD OF VILLANOVA** <note>Arnaldus de Villa Nova (c. 1240–1311), a famous physician and religious reformer whose name was attached to many influential alchemical texts.</note> says: *The stone is not a stone; it is spirit, soul, and body; it is volatile, white as the tears of the eye; if you say it is water, you speak the truth...*

# POLITICAL EXERCISE: WHETHER THEY BE ALCHEMISTS
<note>The title "Political Exercise" refers to a formal academic or legal inquiry into the social and legal status of alchemists within a governed state.</note>

...for the sake of [passing the time], they wished to paint these as if they were cucurbits <note>original: *cucurbitas*. A cucurbit is a gourd-shaped glass vessel used in alchemical distillation, forming the lower part of an alembic.</note>, or that they had hidden certain moral or other common meanings under them when there was no cause for such concealment. They <note>The alchemists and their defenders.</note> wish to believe that the ancients intended to preserve certain greater secrets of nature for those who are wiser by means of these monuments. Such arguments, however, have little appearance of truth and will be of little use in this case.

For first, the interpretation of hieroglyphics—as with all diagrams and images—is quite doubtful and ambiguous, so that nothing certain can be gathered from them. And even if a particular interpretation seems to explain the whole image, I do not see why it should be preferred over another, unless it is proven by clear arguments that the authors of the image intended to indicate this specific meaning rather than another.

Next, I easily grant that the ancient Egyptians were not entirely foolish or lazy; however, it often happens that we, carried away by an excessive love of antiquity, imagine them to have been wiser and more skilled than they actually were. 

I would be even less inclined to assert that they painted these figures merely to pass the time; rather, I am fully convinced that they displayed a portion of their wisdom beneath these veils <note>original: *inuolucris*, literally "wrappings" or "envelopes," a common metaphor for allegorical or symbolic language.</note>. But must it then be immediately concluded that they wove chemical secrets <note>original: *chemica arcana*</note> into these symbols? Why not theological secrets? Why not moral? Why not political? Naturally, it is assumed these other subjects are not to be valued as highly as chemical secrets. But here is the error of the alchemists, pursued with great zeal...

From this, it is not to be wondered at that the same or similar symbols occur in both places—among the chemists and the Egyptians; much less should it be inferred from this that the Egyptians hid chemical secrets under their hieroglyphs.

Blaise de Vigenère (1523–1596) was a French diplomat and alchemist known for his work on ciphers and his chemical interpretations of art.</note> does in his *Commentary on the Tablets of Philostratus* <note>original: *commentario in Philostrati tabulas*. This refers to Vigenère’s 1578 translation and massive commentary on the *Imagines* of Philostratus, which he interpreted through an alchemical lens.</note>, and Pierre-Jean Fabre <note>original: *Petrum Ioannem Fabrum*. Fabre (1588–1658) was a French physician who believed that all ancient myths, including the Iliad and Odyssey, were allegories for the "Great Work" of alchemy.</note> in his *Pan-Chemicus*, as Morhof <note>Daniel Georg Morhof (1639–1691), the German polymath mentioned on the previous page.</note> likewise informs us—rest upon no more certain foundation. 

This is proven by the vastly different interpretations by learned men that are in everyone’s hands: some of whom seem to have found Moses everywhere in mythology, others Joshua, others moral doctrine, others civil law, others natural science, and others something else entirely. I could with equal ease carve both metaphysics and logic out of these stories, or whatever else might come to the mind of someone who thinks it worthwhile to win the authority of antiquity for their own opinions.

### POLITICAL EXERCISES: WHETHER ALCHEMISTS SHOULD BE [TOLERATED]

Even if their credibility <note>The author refers to the esteemed witnesses mentioned on the previous page, such as Van Helmont and Sachs von Löwenheim.</note> should not be called into question in the highest degree, there is nonetheless hardly anyone so cautious and circumspect that the most cunning impostors among the alchemists cannot cast a fog <note>original: *offundere caliginem*; a Latin idiom meaning to deceive or blind someone to the truth.</note> over their eyes. The types of fraud used by these men are infinite and most subtle; for this reason, one should not even trust those who swear under oath that they have seen a base metal <note>original: *ignobilius metallum*; literally "less noble metal," referring to common metals like lead or mercury which alchemists believed could be "exalted" or ennobled into gold.</note> transmuted into gold, until it is certain that they have not been led into error by such an impostor.

But if these and other arguments of the same kind were allowed to stand, what, I ask, would there be that could not be rendered doubtful and uncertain? Suppose that some—indeed, many—among the alchemists either deceive or are deceived; does it follow that they *all* deceive or suffer deception? Who could believe that so many men, separated by such vast distances and so many centuries, could have entered into a conspiracy, as it were, to agree on this: to deceive the world and the human race? I do not claim that this is in no way possible; I do contend, however, that it is extremely difficult to achieve, and thus this consensus cannot be dismissed except by the most serious and weighty reasons.

What, then, are those reasons that lead the haters of alchemy to challenge the credibility of so many men? They are trivial indeed, and truly of no weight. Does Nature perhaps object? But this...

Or, if you do not believe the alchemists themselves, why do you deny credit to those who have witnessed the alchemists' experiments with their own eyes? "They too could have been deceived," you say. What if they employed every possible caution so that they might not be deceived? "This is not established," you say. But there are those who assert this, and affirm it both of themselves and of others. "I do not believe them," you say. Why do you not believe? "Because I do not wish to believe them." For in the end, everything returns to this: a doubt supported by stubbornness and anything other than just reasons, if one rejects all the experiments of alchemists and the historical accounts circulated about them without discrimination.

HERMANN CONRING <note>A prominent 17th-century German physician and polymath who was often skeptical of the mystical claims of alchemy.</note>, (e) being perhaps a bit more unfair toward Paracelsus than is fitting for such a great man, offers various objections to this testimony. *“Truly,” he says, “this is nothing to the point. For alchemists are accustomed to hiding their art with great effort; hence, regarding Paracelsus, it is quite likely that he undertook that transmutation <note>The alchemical process of changing base metals into gold.</note> while his servant was away, so that the secret would not become known to a man whom he perhaps judged unworthy of such a confidence. It is very well known that this has happened to some who were completely ignorant of how to prepare that powder <note>The "powder of projection," a form of the Philosopher's Stone used to transmute base metals into gold.</note>, perhaps with some **spirit** <note>original: *genio*. I fear that it was from such generosity that **Paracelsus** <note>Philippus Aureolus Theophrastus Bombastus von Hohenheim (1493–1541), a famous Swiss physician and alchemist.</note> also occasionally obtained those purses full of coins (1). But these conjectures are of such a kind that, if they are granted any room, then absolutely no example of a base metal being transmuted into gold can be put forward as proof. For what example could be so well-established that an exception would not be ready at hand for those wishing to call its truth into doubt? They might argue that the testimony of one or even several people is not enough; that they could have been deceived, provided they did not intend to deceive others; or that an infernal spirit could have supplied the **gold-making** <note>original Greek: *χρυσοποιὸν* (chrysopoion)</note> powder, and other arguments of that same sort. Let all historical reliability therefore be cast aside; for nothing will be so certain, when it rests on the testimonies of others, that it cannot be shaken and shattered by this line of reasoning.

From this, two types of Erfurt groschen <term>grossi|A thick silver coin widely used in the German states</term> are observed: those without the symbols for sulfur and mercury, and those with them, of which the former are said to be of lesser quality. But it has been observed by some, and confirmed by the testimonies of men worthy of belief (s), that before these particular mint-masters at Erfurt, there was another who made use of these same symbols. Therefore, after the death of Gustavus Adolphus, when the leaders of the Swedish army transferred the minting office from Stettin <note>Original Latin: Sedino</note> to Erfurt, they tasked that mint-master—whose custom it was to distinguish his coins with the characters for sulfur and mercury—with the duty of striking Swedish currency. From this, it is clearly evident why coins bearing the King's image and marked with what appear to be chemical signs were finally struck only after the death of Gustavus Adolphus. 

**SAMUEL REYHER** <note>Samuel Reyher (1635–1714) was a German polymath and professor known for his works on law, mathematics, and numismatics (the study of coins).</note> indeed raises several objections to this point, but they do not settle the matter at all. For first, he attempts to prove that such coins were struck even before the thirty-fourth year of the recently passed century <note>1634</note> by the example of that coin which the second figure displays here. This, however, contributes little to the argument. For it is well established that this coin was also struck after the death of Gustavus Adolphus, as he himself admits; and thus, it cannot be proven from this evidence that the King himself commanded such coins to be struck,

Furthermore, since coins marked with those characters were already being minted at Erfurt long before the King's arrival in Thuringia, and it is established by the certain testimony of trustworthy men that these were simply the personal symbols of the mint-masters, whatever is said about that Erfurt <term>alchemist|alchemista; a practitioner of the ancient art of chemistry and transmutation.</term> collapses of its own accord. Indeed, the frank honesty of <term>WEDEL</term> <note>Georg Wolfgang Wedel (1645–1721) was a prominent German physician, chemist, and professor at Jena who applied scientific rigor to alchemical claims.</note> pleases me; he openly acknowledges that the cause of the alchemists cannot be supported by this reasoning. Indeed, if no other proof of the art were provided, this would be a very weak argument, since such marks could be fashioned according to the whim of the mint-master or for other reasons.*

Now, as for the coin of Frederick I, Duke of Gotha, as well as the one said to have been presented to Emperor Ferdinand III, these will certainly not cause trouble for anyone without reason. This refers to "artificial" gold produced through the philosopher's stone rather than mined from the earth.</note> would need to be demonstrated by much clearer arguments.

Yet, for that reason, it is not as if there is no advantage for the virtuous <note>original: *proborum*; refers to those of upright character and moral integrity</note> over the wicked <note>original: *impiis*; the ungodly or irreverent</note> even in the knowledge of natural things. I indeed believe that, even if we admit the truth of the <term>transmutatory art</term> <note>original: *artis transmutatoriae*; the alchemical process of changing base metals into gold</note>, one should not immediately expect such a bounty of gold as men either hope for or promise themselves. Yet, let us grant something to common opinion and suppose that by this art as much gold could be produced as anyone desired; it would still be the duty of a prudent prince to by no means permit this. For through an excessive abundance, the price <note>original: *pretium*; refers here to both the monetary value and the purchasing power</note> of gold would eventually be debased, from which a great disturbance of all affairs—and especially of commerce—would arise. For the cause of value is to be sought no less in the rarity of a thing than in its utility. Indeed, if we inquire into the reason why the price of things is driven upward, we will find that rarity plays the leading role in the account. Nor can it be otherwise, given the foolish desires of men. For they do not only set a price on those things which serve pleasure and the comforts of life, but <term>ambition</term> <note>original: *ambitio*; here meaning the desire for social status and distinction</note>, which torments mortals, also ensures that they especially value those things which they believe they will share with only a few others. Hence, everywhere, those things that are commonplace and found anywhere are looked down upon as worthless...

And this could finally be easily tolerated in other things, the price of which, whether it be increased or decreased, seems to be a matter of indifference. But as far as gold is concerned—since it constitutes the material of **eminent price** <note>original: *pretii eminentis*; a technical term in 17th-century natural law and economics referring to the universal standard of value that money provides</note>, a function for which not all things can equally serve—it is certainly less to be permitted that its price be too greatly diminished. For those who think, rashly and without compelling reason, that the **nobler metals** <note>i.e., gold and silver</note> were chosen to maintain an "eminent price" by mere whim, are shamefully mistaken. The matter itself teaches that the material of eminent price must be so constituted that, first of all, it contains value in itself due to its **rarity**, so that men do not refuse to exchange other things of value for it. For just as no one accepts a **guarantor** <note>original: *fideiussorem*; a person who legally takes responsibility for another's debt</note> (b) unless he is a man of proven credit and wealthy—whereas in a man of low status there is thought to be little security—so no one would exchange their own property, which they had acquired with great labor or industry, for a thing found everywhere, such as a handful of earth or sand. It was necessary, therefore, for **coinage** <note>original: *nummum*</note> to consist of a material that was both easy to store and in which, because of its rarity, the prices of many things could be, as it were, compressed. To this is added that it must also be compact and solid, so that it is not easily worn down by use and handling

...he fights against authorities, opposing an entire troop of learned doctors to a single opinion: a type of argument that was once frequent in the schools of jurists, but today finds scarcely any place, even if it is heard by the author as an "adamantine foundation" <note>An "adamantine foundation" refers to an unbreakable or rock-solid basis for an argument.</note>. > *“it is certain that there were in previous centuries, and are now, countless serious men who practiced that art and proclaimed that it was profitable for them.”*

...one point concerns those whom they deceive, and the other concerns the whole state <term>commonwealth; Latin: "respublica"</term>. Regarding these victims, it cannot be doubted that the impostors are held to the restitution of the damages they have caused; for among the laws inscribed upon the minds of all people, a primary one is that another person must not be harmed, not even in their property. If someone has caused harm, however, they are completely obligated to repair the damage they have done.

But since it is also in the interest of the state that no one be allowed to defraud others with impunity, a penalty is rightly established against such impostors. This punishment should be lessened or increased depending on the frequency of the crime and the nature of other circumstances that usually come into account here. 

Because that "pseudo-alchemical disease" is so incredibly persistent—meaning those who have once been infected by it rarely stop practicing these arts—it would be neither unfair nor useless to the state to either banish men clearly convicted of such fraud, or certainly to inflict a punishment that strips them of the ability to harm and deceive others again.

From this you may also conclude that, since he never abandoned the hope of producing gold <note>original: "auri conficiendi"; the primary goal of chrysopoeia or gold-making</note>, he did not reach the pinnacle of the art—though there are some who assert he did, as **CHRISTIAN FRANZ PAULLINI** <note>Paullini (1643–1712) was a German physician and polymath known for his extensive correspondence and scholarly works.</note> explains in more detail in the letter we have already praised above (q). Moreover, if a prince sets limits on his curiosity and applies himself to investigating the secrets of nature through the chemical art in such a way that he neglects none of those duties pertaining to the administration of the state <note>original: "reipublicae administrationem"; referring to the "commonwealth" or the public business of the state</note>, he is so far from being blamed that he rather deserves the highest praise. 

Thus **John**, son of **Frederick I**, Elector of Brandenburg, a prince of the mildest character and most fond of the liberal arts, since he delighted in the investigation of natural things, preferred an honorable and liberal leisure to the electoral dignity. After this dignity was transferred to his brother Frederick, John spent his life in the greatest tranquility, contemplating and admiring the works of God. And from that it came to pass that he was distinguished by the nickname **THE ALCHEMIST**, as the venerable man **PHILIP JAKOB SPENER** (r) <note>Spener (1635–1705) was a leading theologian and the founder of Pietism, who also wrote on genealogy and heraldry.</note> testifies. Concerning him, the most celebrated man **CHRISTOPH BECKMANN** (s) also rightly judges that it cannot be turned into a fault against him that he delighted in that art, which comprises a significant part of wis-

He proved his claims through successful trials, transmuting copper and tin into the finest silver.

However, feeling that much was still lacking in his knowledge, and so that he might devote himself to his art with uninterrupted labor, he secretly withdrew to a certain <term>empiric<note>An "empiric" was a practitioner—often a doctor or chemist—who relied on practical experience and observation rather than formal academic theory. At this time, it could also imply a self-taught alchemist.</note></term> named Sibert in a particular suburb. After thirteen weeks had passed there, driven by a lack of necessary funds for his expenses, he sought and obtained permission from his former master to depart. Upon his return, he displayed a far different manner and character, so much so that he appeared to be an entirely different man to those with whom he had previously been familiar. Namely, whereas before he had delighted in vain conversations and other worldly temptations, now his speech and actions breathed nothing but piety. Indeed, while he labored over the transmutation of metals, he himself was being transmuted in spirit. <note>The author uses the metaphor of alchemy to describe a religious or moral conversion, suggesting that as Böttger purified metals, his own soul was being "refined."</note>

Once, having invited two highly-regarded ministers of the church mentioned in Section 19—**Mr. Winckler** and **Mr. Porst** <note>Johann Winckler and Johann Porst were influential Lutheran Pietist theologians in Berlin; their presence suggests Böttger was attempting to prove his work was divinely sanctioned or moral.</note>—when the conversation turned toward alchemy, Bötticher rose from the table after the meal and asked them to go up with him to an upper room. In their presence, along with his host and the host’s wife, he showed them a crucible, asking if they were willing to trust his word. When they replied that the vessel certainly appeared entirely empty to them, he placed it upon the fire and produced a small piece of lead weighing three <term>half-ounces<note>Original: "semuncias." A traditional unit of weight.</note></term>.

# MOSES, THE GOD OF AARON,
### OR
# THE POWER
### AND
# DUTY
## OF PRINCES
### IN SACRED MATTERS,
->From<-
->the canonical Scripture alone<-
->*With a zeal for truth*<-
->demonstrated<-
->by<-
### ALBERT RIPER
-><term>Doctor of Laws<note>original: *I. C.*, an abbreviation for *Juris Consultus*, a title for a legal expert or jurist</note></term><-

---

->Deventer,<-
->IN THE YEAR 1717.<-

<note>The title "Moses, the God of Aaron" refers to the biblical book of Exodus (4:16 and 7:1), where God tells Moses he will be as a "god" to his brother Aaron the priest. In 18th-century political theology, this was often used as a metaphor to argue that the civil ruler (the Prince) holds authority over the religious ministers (the Priesthood).</note>
